problems.title: The order of $g^6$ and $g^{13}$
problems.problem: Let $G$ be any group and $g \in G$ which is not identity. Let $\text{Ord}(g) = 20 $. Then find the order of $g^6$ and $g^{13}$.
problems.solution:
Let us first prove a general result. For any $g \in G$ if $\text{ord}(g) = n $, then for any $k \in \mathbb{N} $, the order of $g^k$ will be $\frac{n}{\gcd (n, k)}$.

To prove the above, we need to show that
  • $\left( g^k \right) ^{\frac{n}{\gcd (n,k)}} = e$ and
  • if $\left( g^k \right) ^j = e$, then $\frac{n}{\gcd{n,k}} \mid j$.
Since $\text{ord}(g) = n$, the first point is clear. \[ \left( g^k \right) ^{\frac{n}{\gcd (n,k)}} = \left( g^n \right) ^{\frac{k}{\gcd (n,k)}} = e. \] For the second point, we note that \[ (g^k)^j = e \implies n \mid kj. \] So we have \begin{align*} n \mid kj \text{ and } n \mid nj & \implies n \mid \gcd (nj, kj) \\ & \implies n \mid \gcd (n,k)j \\ & \implies \frac{n}{\gcd (n,k)} \mid j. \end{align*}
Now using the result that we have just proved we have \begin{align*} \text{ord} \left( g^6 \right) & = \frac{20}{\gcd (20,6)} = \frac{20}{2} = 10 \\[2ex] \text{ord}\left( g^{13} \right) & = \frac{20}{\gcd (20, 13)} = \frac{20}{1} = 20. \end{align*}

problems.title: The nilpotent elements of a commutative ring form a subring
problems.problem: An element $a$ in a ring is said to be nilpotent if there exists $k\in \mathbb{N} $ such that $a^k = 0$. Show that the nilpotent elements of a commutative ring form a subring.
problems.solution:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and \[ \mathcal{N} \coloneqq \left\{ r \in R : \exists~ n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } r^n = 0 \right\}. \] We claim that $\mathcal{N} $ is a subring of $R$. Let $r_1, r_2\in \mathcal{N} $. This means there exist positive integers $n_1$ and $n_2$ such that $r_1^{n_1} = 0 = r_2^{n_2}$. Note that if $r^k = 0$, then $(-r)^k = 0$, so $\mathcal{N} $ is closed under additive inverse. Consider \begin{align*} \left( r_1 - r_2 \right) ^{n_1 + n_2} & = \sum_{i=0}^{n_1 + n_2} \binom{n_1 + n_2}{i} r_1^{n_1 + n_2 - i} (-r_2)^i \\ & = \sum_{i=0}^{n_2} \binom{n_1 + n_2}{i} r_1^{n_1 + n_2 - i} (-r_2)^{i} + \sum_{i=n_2}^{n_1 + n_2} r_1^{n_1 + n_2 - i} (-r_2)^i. \end{align*} Since for any $0 \leq i \leq n_2$ we have $n_1 \lt n_1 + n_2 - i \lt n_1 + n_2$, and therefore, $r_1^{n_1 + n_2 - i} = 0$. Similarly, $(-r_2)^{i} = 0$. Thus, $(r_1 - r_2)^{n_1 + n_2} = 0$. Hence, $r_1 - r_2 \in \mathcal{N} $.
Now we will show that the product of $r_1$ and $r_2$ is also nilpotent. Recall that for a commutative ring $(ab)^k = a^k b^k$. So we have \begin{align*} (r_1 r_2)^{n_1} = r_1^{n_1} r_2^{n_2} = 0. \end{align*} Thus, $\mathcal{N} $ is closed under multiplication and hence $\mathcal{N} $ is a subring of $R$.

problems.title: Centralizer of group element is a subgroup
problems.problem: Fix an element $h$ in a multiplicative group $G$. Recall that the centralizer of $h$ in $G$ is \[ C(h) = \left\{ g\in G: gh = hg \right\} . \] Prove that $C(h)$ is a subgroup of $G$. Conclude that the group generated by $h$, $\langle h \rangle $ is a subgroup of $C(h)$.
problems.solution:
We will show the centralizer of $h$ is a subgroup of $G$. We need to show that given any $a,b \in C(h)$, $ab^{-1} \in C(h)$. Note that $a\in G$ so it must have an inverse in $G$. \begin{align*} ha = ah \implies a = h^{-1} ah \implies a^{-1} = h^{-1} a^{-1} h. \end{align*} Now we have \begin{align*} h\left( ab^{-1} \right) = (ha) b^{-1} = a \left( hb^{-1} \right) = a \left( h (h^{-1}b^{-1} h ) \right) = ab^{-1} h. \end{align*} Thus, $ab^{-1} \in C(h)$ and hence it is a subgroup of $G$.
As we know that $\langle h \rangle $ is a subgroup of $G$. In order to show it is a subgroup of $C(h)$ it is enough to show that $\langle h \rangle \subseteq C(h)$. Note that for any $h \in C(h)$ and $C(h)$ is a subgroup, so for any $k \in \mathbb{Z} $, $h^k \in C(h)$.

problems.title: Number of distinct subgroups of order 7
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a group with exactly $36$ elements of order $7$. How many distinct subgroups of order $7$ does $G$ have?
problems.solution: Note that if $g \in G$ such that $\text{ord}(g) = 7 $, then the subgroup generated by $g$, $\{ 1,g,g^2, \dots,g^6 \} $ has order $7$. Also, since $7$ is prime, the order of each $g^i$, for $i =1, 2, \dots,6$ will be $7$. Therefore, each subgroup of $G$ of order $7$ contains exactly $6$ distinct elements of order $7$. Since $G$ has exactly $36$ elements of order $7$, the number of subgroups of $G$ of order $7$ is $\frac{36}{6}= 6$.

problems.title: Prove that $(x + y)^{p^n} = x^{p^n} + y^{p^n}$
problems.problem: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $p$ be a prime number. Also assume that $\text{char}(R)=p $. Let $x,y\in R$. Prove that $(x + y)^{p^n} = x^{p^n} + y^{p^n}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N} $.
problems.solution: We will use the binomial expansion theorem. Recall that \[ (x + y)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} x^k y^{n-k}. \] We have \begin{align*} (x + y)^{p^n} & = \sum_{k=0}^{p^n} \binom{p^n}{k}x^k y^{p^n - k} \\ & = = x^{p^n} + \sum_{k=1}^{p^n - 1} \binom{p^n}{k}x^k y^{p^n - k} + y^{p^n}. \end{align*} Note that for each $1 \leq k \leq p^n - 1$, the term $\binom{p^n}{k}$ is divisible by $p$ Since the ring has characteristic $p$, all the term vanishes. Therefore, \[ (x + y)^{p^n} = x^{p^n} + y^{p^n}. \]

problems.title: Prime and maximal ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[x]
problems.problem:
Prove that
    \[
        I = \left\{ f(x) \in \mathbb{Z} [x] : f(-3) = 0 \right\}
    \] 
        is a prime ideal of $\mathbb{Z} [x]$. Check if it is a maximal ideal of $\mathbb{Z} [x]$.
problems.solution:
We will the following characterization of the prime ideal. In a commutative ring $R$, an ideal $\mathcal{P} $ is a prime ideal if and only if $R/\mathcal{P} $ is an integral domain. It is a field if and only if $\mathcal{P} $ is a maximal ideal. \vf \hf Consider the following map: \[ \varphi : \mathbb{Z} [x] \to \mathbb{Z} ,~ f(x) \to f(-3). \] For any $f,g\in \mathbb{Z} [x]$, we have
  1. $\varphi (f+g) = (f+g)(-3) = f(-3) = g(-3) = \varphi (f) + \varphi (g)$.
  2. $\varphi (fg) = (fg)(-3) = f(-3) g(-3) = \varphi (f) \varphi (g)$.
Therefore, $\varphi $ is a ring homomorphism. Now for any integer $k$, consider the constant polynomial $f(x) = k$. Then $\varphi (f) = f(-3) = k$. Hence, $\varphi $ is surjective. Note that \[ \ker \varphi = \left\{ f \in \mathbb{Z} [x] : \varphi (f) = f(-3) = 0 \right\} = I. \] Therefore, by the first isomorphism theorem \[ \mathbb{Z}[x]/I \cong \mathbb{Z} , \] which is an integral domain. Thus, $I$ is a prime ideal. Since, the quotient is not a field, $I$ is not a maximal ideal.

problems.title: Algebraically closed field is infinite
problems.problem: A field $\mathbb{F} $ is said to be an algebraically closed field if each non-constant polynomial in $\mathbb{F} [x]$ has a root in $\mathbb{F} $. Show that $\mathbb{R} $ is not algebraically closed. Prove that any algebraically closed field is infinite.
problems.solution:
To show that $\mathbb{R} $ is not algebraically closed, we need to find a polynomial in $\mathbb{R} [x]$ which does not have a zero in $\mathbb{R} $. The polynomial $p(x) = x^2 + 1$ does not have a zero in $\mathbb{R} [x]$ and hence, $\mathbb{R} $ is not algebraically closed.
Let $\mathbb{F} $ be an algebraically closed field. We need to show that an $\mathbb{F} $ is infinite. Let us assume that $\mathbb{F} $ is a finite field with $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ elements. Consider the polynomial \[ p(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n \left( x - a_i \right) + 1. \] Since the coefficient of $p(x)$ lies in $\mathbb{F} [x]$, it is clear that $p(x) \in \mathbb{F} [x]$. But note that for each $i= 1,2,\dots,n$ \[ p\left( a_i \right) = 1 \neq 0. \] Thus, $p(x)$ does not have a root in $\mathbb{F} [x]$, which gives a contradiction to the fact that $\mathbb{F} $ is an algebraically closed field. Thus, $\mathbb{F} $ must be an infinite field.

problems.title: A problem on group theory, GATE 2023
problems.problem:
Let $GL_2(\mathbb{C} )$ denote the group of $2\times 2$ invertible complex matrices with usual matrix multiplication. For $S,T \in GL_2(\mathbb{C} ),\ \langle S, T \rangle $ denotes the subgroup generated by $S$ and $T$. Let $S = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} \in GL_2(\mathbb{C} )$ and $G_1, G_2, G_3$ be three subgroups of $GL_2(\mathbb{C} )$ given by \begin{align*} G_1 & = \langle S, T_1 \rangle , \text{ where } T_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \iota & 0 \\ 0 & \iota \\ \end{bmatrix}, \\ G_2 & = \langle S, T_2 \rangle , \text{ where } T_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \iota & 0 \\ 0 & -\iota \\ \end{bmatrix}, \\ G_3 & = \langle S, T_3 \rangle , \text{ where } T_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Let $Z\left( G_i \right) $ denote the center of $G_i$ for $i = 1,2,3$. Which of the following statements is correct?
  • $G_1$ is isomorphic to $G_3$
  • $Z\left( G_1 \right) $ is isomorphic to $Z \left( G_2 \right) $
  • a$Z\left( G_3 \right) = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} \right\} $
  • $Z\left( G_2 \right) $ is isomorphic to $Z\left( G_3 \right) $
problems.solution:
We recall that the center of a group $G$ is defined as \[ Z(G) \coloneqq \left\{ g\in G : g g^\prime = g^\prime g \ \text{for all } g^\prime \in G \right\}. \] We have the following important properties for the center of a group.
  • A group $ G $ is abelian if and only if $Z(G) = G$.
  • If the group is generated by $g_1,g_2,\dots, g_k$, then \[ Z(G) = \left\{ g \in G : g g_j = g_j g\ \text{for } j = 1,2,\dots, k \right\} . \] Since each $g\in G$ can be written as the product of $g_i$'s, we have, if $g_i g_j= g_j g_i$ for all $i,j \in \{ 1,2,\dots, k \} $, then $Z(G) = G$, that is, $G$ is abelian.
Let us find the center of each of these groups. Note that \[ Z \left( G_j \right) = \left\{ A \in GL_2(\mathbb{C} ) : A S = S A \text{ and } A T_j = T_j A ,\ j = 1,2,3 \right\} . \] Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Consider the first condition, that is, $AS = SA$. \begin{align*} AS = SA & \implies \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \\ \end{bmatrix} \\[1ex] & \implies \begin{bmatrix} b & -a \\ d & -c \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -c & -d \\ a & b \\ \end{bmatrix} \\[1ex] & \implies b = -c, a = d. \end{align*} Thus, the matrix $A$ reduces to \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \\ \end{bmatrix}. \]
Now for each $T_j$, we need the commutative property to be satisfied. Note that, \[ T_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \iota & 0 \\ 0 & \iota \\ \end{bmatrix} = \iota I_2 \implies A T_1 = \iota A = T_1 A,\ \forall\ A. \] In particular, $S T_1 = T_1 S$ and hence, $Z\left( G_1 \right) = G_1$, that is, $G_1$ is abelian.
Now we consider $T_2$. \begin{align*} \textcolor{red}{j = 2} & \implies A T_2 = T_2 A \\ & \implies \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \iota & 0 \\ 0 & -\iota \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \iota & 0 \\ 0 & -\iota \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \\ \end{bmatrix} \\[1ex] & \implies \begin{bmatrix} a \iota & -b \iota \\ -b \iota & -a \iota \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a \iota & b \iota \\ b \iota & -a \iota \\ \end{bmatrix} \\[1ex] & \implies b = -b \text{ that is},\ b = 0 \\ & \implies A = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & a \\ \end{bmatrix} = a I_2. \end{align*} Since $\det S = \det T_2 = 1$ and $A = a I_2 \in \left\langle S, T_2 \right\rangle $ implies $\det \left( a I_2 \right) = 1$, that is $a = \pm 1$. So, the only possibility for $A$ to be either $\pm I_2$. Since, $S^2 = -I_2$, so \[ Z\left\{ G_2 \right\} = \left\{ \pm I_2 \right\} . \]
Finally, \begin{align*} \textcolor{red}{j = 3} & \implies A T_3 = T_3 A \\ & \implies \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \\ \end{bmatrix} \\[1ex] & \implies \begin{bmatrix} b & a \\ a & -b \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -b & a \\ a & b \\ \end{bmatrix} \\[1ex] & \implies b = -b \text{ that is, } b = 0 \\ & \implies A = a I_2. \end{align*} Here again, since $S, T_3 \in GL_2(\mathbb{R} ) \subseteq GL_2(\mathbb{C} )$ and $\det S = 1$ and $\det T_3 = -1$, therefore, $aI_2 \in G_3 = \left\langle S, T_3 \right\rangle \subseteq GL_2(\mathbb{R} ) $. This implies $\det a I_2 = 1$ and hence, $a = \pm 1$. Since $S^2 = -I_2$, so \[ Z\left( G_3 \right) = \left\{ \pm I_2 \right\} . \]
In summary, we got
  • $Z\left( G_1 \right) = G_1$, that is, $G_1$ is abelian.
  • $Z\left( G_2 \right) = \{ \pm I_2 \} \neq G_2$, so $G_2$ is not abelian.
  • $Z\left( G_3 \right) = \{ \pm I_2 \} \neq G_3$, so $G_2$ is not abelian.
Therefore, options (a), (b) and (c) are FALSE and option (d) is TRUE.

problems.title: Check if the polynomial is irreducible over Q
problems.problem: Check if the polynomial $p(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 -8$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q} $.
problems.solution: We recall that $p(x) \in \mathbb{Z} [x]$ is irreducible (reducible) in $\mathbb{Q} $ if and only if it is irreducible (reducible) in $\mathbb{Z} $. Since, the degree of the polynomial $p(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 -8$ is $3$, it is reducible if and only if it has a root in $\mathbb{Z} $. Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z} $ be a root of $p(x)$. This implies $\alpha ^3 + 3 \alpha ^2 - 8 = 0 $ and hence $\alpha $ must divide $8$. The possible roots of $p(x)$ are $\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 4, \pm 8$. Now we will compute the value of $p$ at each of these integers. \begin{align*} p(-1) & = 6 \neq 0 \text{ and } (1) = -4 \neq 0 \\ p(-2) & = 59 \neq 0 \text{ and } (2) = -57 \neq 0 \\ p(-4) & = 501 \neq 0 \text{ and } (4) = -499 \neq 0 \\ p(-8) & = 4073 \neq 0 \text{ and } (8) = -4071 \neq 0 \\ \end{align*} Thus, the polynomial is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z} $ and hence $\mathbb{Q} $.

problems.title: Finding the center of the group
problems.problem: Let $G$ be the set of all real matrices of the following form: \[ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a & b \\ 0 & 1 & c \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix},\ \ a,b,c \in \mathbb{R}. \] Prove that $G$ is a group under matrix multiplication and find the center of $G$, that is, the set of all elements $g \in G$ such that $gh = hg$ for all $h \in G$.
problems.solution:
Let $A, B \in G$. Let \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a_1 & a_2 \\ 0 & 1 & a_3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \text{ and } B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & b_1 & b_2 \\ 0 & 1 & b_3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}. \] Then, the multiplication \[ AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & b_1 + a_1 & b_2 + a_1 b_3 + a_2 \\ 0 & 1 & b_3 + a_3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \in G. \] Since, matrix multiplication is associative, for any $A,B,C \in G$ we have $A(BC) = (AB)C$. Clearly, the identity matrix is an element of $G$. Now for the inverse of $A$, we multiply by any matrix $B \in G$ and solve for the unknowns. Let $A$ and $B$ be as given above. \begin{align*} A B = I & \implies b_1 + a_1 = 0,\ b_2 + a_1 b_3 + a_2 = 0 \text{ and } b_3 + a_3 = 0 \\ & \implies b_1 = -a_1,\ b_3 = -a_3 \ \text{ and } b_2 = -a_1(-a_3) - a_2 = a_1 a_3 - a_2. \end{align*} Therefore, the inverse of $A$ will be \[ A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -a_1 & a_1 a_3 - a_2 \\ 0 & 1 & -a_3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}. \] Thus, $G$ is a group under matrix multiplication.
Now we need to determine the center of $G$. Let $Z(G)$ denote the center of $G$, then \[ Z(G) = \left\{ B \in G: AB = BA ,~ A \in G \right\}. \] Let $A \in Z(G)$. Then $A$ commutes with every element of $G$. We take $B\in G$ and find conditions on $a_1, a_2$ and $a_3.$ \begin{align*} & AB = BA \\ \implies & \begin{bmatrix} 1 & b_1 + a_1 & b_2 + a_1 b_3 + a_2 \\ 0 & 1 & b_3 + a_3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a_1 + b_1 & a_2 + b_1 a_3 + b_2 \\ 0 & 1 & a_3 + b_3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \\ \implies & b_1 + a_1 b_3 + a_2 = a_2 + b_1 a_3 + b_2 \\ \implies & a_1 b_3 = b_1 a_3. \end{align*} With the help of the condition, we take two matrices, one with $b_1 = 0$ and $b_3 \neq 0$ and other $b_3 = 0$ and $b_1 \neq 0 $. If $b_1 = 0$ and $b_3 \neq 0$, then we have $a_1 = 0$. Similarly, if $b_1 \neq 0$ and $b_3 = 0$, then $a_3 = 0$. Therefore, the center of the group will be \[ Z(G) = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & a \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}: a \in \mathbb{R} \right\} . \]

problems.title: Intersection of normal subgroup is a normal subgroup
problems.problem: Show that the intersection of two normal subgroups of $G$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
problems.solution: Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be two normal subgroups of $G$. We need to show that $N_1 \cap N_2$ is normal subgroup of $G$. We know that $N \coloneqq N_1 \cap N_2$ is a subgroup. To show, it is normal subgroup, take $g \in G$. We need to show that $gNg^{-1} \subseteq N$. For any $n \in N = N_1 \cap N_2$, we know that $gng^{-1} \in N_1 $ and $gng^{-1} \in N_2$, therefore, $gng^{-1} \in N$. Thus, $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.

problems.title: The element $x \in IJ$ cannot be written as $x = f(x) g(x)$, where $f(x) \in I$ and $g(x) \in J$
problems.problem:
Let $I=(x,2)$ and $J=(x,3)$ be ideal in the ring $\mathbb{Z} [x]$.
  • Prove that $IJ = (x,6)$.
  • Prove that the element $x \in IJ$ cannot be written as $x = f(x) g(x)$, where $f(x) \in I$ and $g(x) \in J$.
problems.solution:
Recall that if $I=(a_1,\dots, a_m)$ and $J=(b_1, \dots, b_n)$ are ideals in a commutative ring, then we have \[ IJ=(a_ib_j), \] where $1\leq i \leq m$ and $1\leq j \leq n$.
  • Using the above fact, we have \[ IJ = \left( x^2, 2x, 3x, 6 \right). \] Since $2x, 3x \in IJ$, so $3x - 2x = x \in IJ$. Thus, the first three generators can be generated by $x$ and hence, \[ IJ = (x, 6). \]
  • Since $\deg (fg) = \deg (f) + \deg (g)$, so if $x = f(x) g(x)$, then either of the function has to be constant. If $f(x) $ is constant, then $f \equiv 2$. Thus, $x = 2g(x)$ which implies $g(x) = 2^{-1} x$. But $2$ is not invertible in $\mathbb{Z} $ and hence $2^{-1} x \notin \mathbb{Z} [x]$, therefore $f \equiv 2$ is not possible. Similarly, if $g(x)$ is constant then $g\equiv 3$ which is also not possible as $3$ is not invertible in $\mathbb{Z} $. Thus $x = f(x) g(x)$ is not possible for any $f(x) \in I$ and $g(x) \in J$.

    We can also solve this by using that $\mathbb{Z} [x]$ is UFD. So, $x = (\pm 1)(\pm x) $. Thus, $f(x) = \pm 1$ and $g(x) = \pm x$ or $f(x) = \pm x$ and $g(x) \pm 1$. In any case, either $1 \in I$ or $1 \in J$ which implies either $I = \mathbb{Z} [x]$ or $J = \mathbb{Z} [x]$ which is not true. Thus, we can not write $x$ as a product of elements from $I$ and $J$.

problems.title: The quaternion group $Q_8$ is non-abelian but all its subgroups are normal
problems.problem:
Let $Q_8 = \{ \pm 1, \pm i, \pm j, \pm k \}$ be the quaternion group, with
    \[
        i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1,
    \]
    where $-1$ commutes with everything. Show that $Q_8$ is not abelian, find all of its subgroups, and show that every subgroup of $Q_8$ is normal.
problems.hint:
• From $ijk = -1$ deduce $ij = k$ and $ji = -k$.
  • By Lagrange's theorem a subgroup has order $1, 2, 4$ or $8$. How many elements of order $2$ does $Q_8$ have? A subgroup of index $2$ is always normal.
problems.solution:
Not abelian. Multiplying $ijk = -1$ on the right by $k$ gives $ij \cdot k^2 = -k$, i.e. $-ij = -k$, so $ij = k$. Similarly $jk = i$ and $ki = j$. Then \[ ji = j (jk) = j^2 k = -k \neq k = ij. \]
Orders of elements. $1$ has order $1$; $-1$ has order $2$; each of $\pm i, \pm j, \pm k$ has order $4$, since its square is $-1$. So $-1$ is the only element of order $2$.
All subgroups. By Lagrange's theorem the possible orders are $1, 2, 4, 8$.
  1. Order $1$: $\{ 1 \}$. Order $8$: $Q_8$.
  2. Order $2$: it must be $\{ 1, x \}$ with $x$ of order $2$, so it is $\{ \pm 1 \}$.
  3. Order $4$: a group of order $4$ is either cyclic or has three elements of order $2$. The second is impossible here, so the subgroup is generated by an element of order $4$, giving $\langle i \rangle = \{ \pm 1, \pm i \}$, $\langle j \rangle = \{ \pm 1, \pm j \}$, $\langle k \rangle = \{ \pm 1, \pm k \}$.
So $Q_8$ has exactly six subgroups.
All are normal. $\{ 1 \}$ and $Q_8$ are normal. $\{ \pm 1 \}$ is normal because $-1$ commutes with every element, so $g\{ \pm 1 \}g^{-1} = \{ \pm 1 \}$ (in fact $\{ \pm 1 \}$ is the centre of $Q_8$). The three subgroups of order $4$ have index $2$, and a subgroup $H$ of index $2$ is always normal: its two left cosets are $H$ and $G \setminus H$, and so are its two right cosets, hence $gH = Hg$ for every $g$.
So $Q_8$ is a non-abelian group in which every subgroup is normal; it is the smallest such group. In an abelian group every subgroup is normal, so "all subgroups normal" does not force a group to be abelian.

problems.title: The additive group $(\mathbb{Q}, +)$ is not finitely generated
problems.problem: Prove that the group $(\mathbb{Q}, +)$ is not cyclic. More generally, prove that it is not finitely generated: there are no finitely many rationals $q_1, \dots, q_n$ such that every rational number is an integer combination $m_1 q_1 + \dots + m_n q_n$.
problems.hint: • Put the generators over a common denominator $b$. Which rationals can then be integer combinations of them?
problems.solution:
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $\mathbb{Q} = \langle q_1, \dots, q_n \rangle$ for some $n \geq 1$. Write $q_i = \frac{a_i}{b_i}$ with $a_i, b_i \in \mathbb{Z}$, $b_i > 0$, and let $b = b_1 b_2 \cdots b_n$. Then each $q_i = \frac{c_i}{b}$ for some integer $c_i$.
Every element of $\langle q_1, \dots, q_n \rangle$ is an integer combination \[ m_1 q_1 + \dots + m_n q_n = \frac{m_1 c_1 + \dots + m_n c_n}{b}, \] so it has the form $\frac{m}{b}$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$. But $\frac{1}{2b} \in \mathbb{Q}$, and $\frac{1}{2b} = \frac{m}{b}$ would give $m = \frac{1}{2} \notin \mathbb{Z}$. This contradiction shows that $\mathbb{Q}$ is not finitely generated.
Taking $n = 1$ shows in particular that $(\mathbb{Q}, +)$ is not cyclic. (By contrast, every finitely generated subgroup of $\mathbb{Q}$ is cyclic: the argument shows it lies inside $\frac{1}{b}\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{Z}$, and subgroups of a cyclic group are cyclic.)

problems.title: Find all ring homomorphisms from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}_6$
problems.problem: Find all ring homomorphisms $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_6$. (Do not assume that $f(1) = 1$.) Which of them send $1$ to $1$?
problems.hint: • A ring homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}$ is determined by $e = f(1)$. Apply $f$ to $1 = 1 \cdot 1$.
problems.solution:
Let $f$ be a ring homomorphism and $e = f(1)$. Additivity forces $f(n) = n e$ for every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, so $f$ is determined by $e$. Multiplicativity applied to $1 = 1 \cdot 1$ gives \[ e = f(1) = f(1)^2 = e^2. \] Conversely, if $e^2 = e$, then $f(n) = ne$ is additive and $f(m) f(n) = mn e^2 = mn e = f(mn)$, so it is a ring homomorphism.
So the ring homomorphisms correspond to the idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}_6$. Checking squares modulo $6$: \[ 0^2 = 0, \quad 1^2 = 1, \quad 2^2 = 4, \quad 3^2 = 9 \equiv 3, \quad 4^2 = 16 \equiv 4, \quad 5^2 = 25 \equiv 1. \] The idempotents are $0, 1, 3, 4$. Hence there are exactly four ring homomorphisms: \[ f_0(n) = 0, \qquad f_1(n) = n, \qquad f_3(n) = 3n, \qquad f_4(n) = 4n \pmod 6. \]
Only $f_1$ sends $1$ to $1$. The images are $\{ 0 \}$, $\mathbb{Z}_6$, $\{ 0, 3 \} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\{ 0, 2, 4 \} \cong \mathbb{Z}_3$ respectively; the last two reflect the decomposition $\mathbb{Z}_6 \cong \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_3$, in which $3$ and $4$ are the identities of the two factors.

problems.title: Finite groups with more than two elements ahs an element with prime order
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a finite group with more than one element. Show that $G$ has an element of prime order.
problems.solution: Since the group has at least two elements, take $g \in G$ which is not identity. Since $G$ is a finite group, $g^n = e$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N} $. Further assume that $n$ is the order of $g$. If $n$ is a prime, we are done. If not, let $p$ be a prime factor of $n$, so $ n = pk$ for $k \in \mathbb{N} $. Thus, \[ e = g^n = g^{pk} = \left( g^k \right) ^p. \] Let $h = g^k$, so we have $h^p = e$. Now we claim that the order of $h$ is $p$. It is clear that $\mathrm{ord}(h) \leq p $. If $\mathrm{ord} (b) = m < p$, then \[ e = b^m = \left( a^k \right) ^m = a^{km}, \] which is a contradiction to $ord(a) = n > km$. Hence, $\mathrm{ord} (b) = p$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.4.5 - Left cosets are the classes of $a \sim b \iff a^{-1} b \in H$
problems.problem:
Let $G$ be a group and $H$ a subgroup of $G$. Define, for $a, b \in G$, $a \sim b$ if $a^{-1} b \in H$. Prove that this defines an equivalence relation on $G$, and show that the equivalence class of $a$ is
    \[
        [a] = aH = \{ ah : h \in H \}.
    \]
    (The sets $aH$ are called the left cosets of $H$ in $G$.)
problems.hint: • Each of the three properties uses one of the subgroup properties: $e \in H$, closure under inverses, closure under products.
problems.solution:
Reflexive: $a^{-1} a = e \in H$, so $a \sim a$.
Symmetric: if $a^{-1} b \in H$, then $b^{-1} a = (a^{-1} b)^{-1} \in H$, so $b \sim a$.
Transitive: if $a^{-1} b \in H$ and $b^{-1} c \in H$, then $a^{-1} c = (a^{-1} b)(b^{-1} c) \in H$, so $a \sim c$.
The classes. For $b \in G$, \[ b \in [a] \iff a^{-1} b \in H \iff a^{-1} b = h \text{ for some } h \in H \iff b = ah \text{ for some } h \in H \iff b \in aH. \] Hence $[a] = aH$.
Since equivalence classes partition $G$, the left cosets of $H$ partition $G$: any two are either equal or disjoint. Moreover $h \mapsto ah$ is a bijection $H \to aH$, so for finite $G$ all cosets have $\vert H \vert$ elements, which is the heart of Lagrange's theorem.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.4.6 - Left and right cosets of $H = \{ i, f \}$ in $S_3$
problems.problem: Let $G = S_3$ and $H = \{ i, f \}$, where $f : S \to S$ is defined by $f(x_1) = x_2$, $f(x_2) = x_1$, $f(x_3) = x_3$. List all the right cosets of $H$ in $G$ and all the left cosets of $H$ in $G$.
problems.hint: • In cycle notation $f = (1\ 2)$. Let $g = (1\ 2\ 3)$; then $S_3 = \{ i, g, g^2, f, fg, fg^2 \}$. Compute the products $gf$, $g^2 f$, $fg$, $fg^2$ (composing from right to left).
problems.solution:
Write permutations of $\{ x_1, x_2, x_3 \}$ by the indices, and compose from right to left ($\sigma\tau$ means "first $\tau$, then $\sigma$"). Then $f = (1\ 2)$; let $g = (1\ 2\ 3)$, so $g^2 = (1\ 3\ 2)$. Computing, \[ fg = (2\ 3), \qquad fg^2 = (1\ 3), \qquad gf = (1\ 3), \qquad g^2 f = (2\ 3). \] (For instance, $fg$: $1 \xrightarrow{g} 2 \xrightarrow{f} 1$, $2 \xrightarrow{g} 3 \xrightarrow{f} 3$, $3 \xrightarrow{g} 1 \xrightarrow{f} 2$, so $fg = (2\ 3)$.) Thus $S_3 = \{ i, g, g^2, f, fg, fg^2 \}$.
Right cosets $Ha = \{ a, fa \}$: \[ H = \{ i, (1\ 2) \}, \qquad Hg = \{ (1\ 2\ 3), (2\ 3) \}, \qquad Hg^2 = \{ (1\ 3\ 2), (1\ 3) \}. \]
Left cosets $aH = \{ a, af \}$: \[ H = \{ i, (1\ 2) \}, \qquad gH = \{ (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3) \}, \qquad g^2 H = \{ (1\ 3\ 2), (2\ 3) \}. \]
In each case there are $3 = \frac{6}{2}$ cosets, of two elements each, and they partition $S_3$. Note that $Hg \neq gH$: the right and left cosets of this $H$ are different, apart from $H$ itself (see the next exercise).

problems.title: Herstein - 2.4.7 - Is every right coset of $H = \{ i, f \}$ in $S_3$ also a left coset?
problems.problem: In the previous exercise ($G = S_3$, $H = \{ i, f \}$ with $f = (1\ 2)$), is every right coset of $H$ in $G$ also a left coset of $H$ in $G$?
problems.hint: • Compare the lists of right and left cosets found in Exercise 2.4.6.
problems.solution:
No. From Exercise 2.4.6 (with $g = (1\ 2\ 3)$), the right cosets are \[ \{ i, (1\ 2) \}, \quad \{ (1\ 2\ 3), (2\ 3) \}, \quad \{ (1\ 3\ 2), (1\ 3) \}, \] and the left cosets are \[ \{ i, (1\ 2) \}, \quad \{ (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3) \}, \quad \{ (1\ 3\ 2), (2\ 3) \}. \]
The right coset $Hg = \{ (1\ 2\ 3), (2\ 3) \}$ is not a left coset: the only left coset containing $(1\ 2\ 3)$ is $gH = \{ (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3) \}$ (left cosets are disjoint), and $gH \neq Hg$. Only $H$ itself is both a left and a right coset.
By the next exercise this means that $H$ is not a normal subgroup of $S_3$: indeed $g H g^{-1} = \{ i, g f g^{-1} \} = \{ i, (2\ 3) \} \neq H$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.4.8 - If every right coset is a left coset, then $aHa^{-1} = H$
problems.problem: Let $H$ be a subgroup of a group $G$. If every right coset of $H$ in $G$ is a left coset of $H$ in $G$, prove that $aHa^{-1} = H$ for all $a \in G$.
problems.hint: • The right coset $Ha$ and the left coset $aH$ both contain $a$. Two left cosets that share an element are equal.
problems.solution:
Let $a \in G$. By hypothesis the right coset $Ha$ is a left coset, say $Ha = bH$. Since $a = ea \in Ha$, we have $a \in bH$. But also $a = ae \in aH$. Left cosets are equivalence classes (Exercise 2.4.5), so two left cosets with a common element are equal: $bH = aH$. Hence \[ Ha = aH \qquad \text{for every } a \in G. \]
Now $aHa^{-1} = (aH)a^{-1} = (Ha)a^{-1} = H(aa^{-1}) = H$. Explicitly: for $h \in H$, $ah \in aH = Ha$, so $ah = h'a$ for some $h' \in H$ and $aha^{-1} = h' \in H$; this shows $aHa^{-1} \subseteq H$, and applying it to $a^{-1}$ gives $a^{-1}Ha \subseteq H$, i.e. $H \subseteq aHa^{-1}$.
So $H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$. Conversely, if $aHa^{-1} = H$ for all $a$, then $aH = Ha$ for all $a$, so every right coset is a left coset. Exercise 2.4.7 shows that this can fail.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.16 - A group with no proper subgroups is cyclic of prime order
problems.problem: If $G$ has no proper subgroups, prove that $G$ is cyclic of order $p$, where $p$ is a prime number. (This sharpens the result of Problem 14.)
problems.hint: • By Problem 14, $G = \langle a \rangle$. Rule out $G$ infinite (look at $\langle a^2 \rangle$) and $\vert G \vert = rs$ with $1 \lt r \lt \vert G \vert$ (look at $\langle a^r \rangle$).
problems.solution:
Here "proper" means different from $(e)$ and from $G$, and we assume $G eq (e)$ (the trivial group is cyclic of order $1$). Take $a \in G$, $a eq e$. Then $\langle a angle eq (e)$, so $\langle a angle = G$: $G$ is cyclic (Problem 14).
$G$ is finite. Suppose $a$ had infinite order. Then $H = \langle a^2 angle$ is a subgroup with $H eq (e)$. Also $a otin H$: if $a = a^{2k}$ then $a^{2k - 1} = e$ with $2k - 1 eq 0$, impossible for an element of infinite order. So $H eq G$, a proper subgroup, a contradiction. Hence $G$ is finite, say $\vert G \vert = n = o(a)$, with $n > 1$.
$n$ is prime. Suppose $n = rs$ with $1 \lt r \lt n$ (so $1 \lt s \lt n$). Let $b = a^r$. Then $b^s = a^{rs} = e$, while for $1 \leq j \lt s$, $b^j = a^{rj} eq e$ because $0 \lt rj \lt n = o(a)$. So $o(b) = s$ and $\langle b angle$ has exactly $s$ elements, with $1 \lt s \lt n$: a proper subgroup, a contradiction. Hence $n$ is a prime $p$, and $G$ is cyclic of order $p$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.17 - The centralizer of a conjugate: $C(x^{-1}ax) = x^{-1}C(a)x$
problems.problem: If $G$ is a group and $a, x \in G$, prove that $C(x^{-1}ax) = x^{-1}C(a)x$. (Here $C(b) = \{ g \in G : gb = bg \}$ is the centralizer of $b$, and $x^{-1}C(a)x = \{ x^{-1}gx : g \in C(a) \}$.)
problems.hint: • $g$ commutes with $x^{-1}ax$ if and only if $xgx^{-1}$ commutes with $a$.
problems.solution:
For $g \in G$, multiplying on the left by $x$ and on the right by $x^{-1}$ (which is reversible), \[ g\,(x^{-1}ax) = (x^{-1}ax)\,g \iff (xgx^{-1})\,a = a\,(xgx^{-1}). \] (Indeed $x\,(g x^{-1} a x)\,x^{-1} = (xgx^{-1})\,a$ and $x\,(x^{-1} a x g)\,x^{-1} = a\,(xgx^{-1})$.)
Therefore \[ g \in C(x^{-1}ax) \iff xgx^{-1} \in C(a) \iff g \in x^{-1}C(a)x, \] where the last step holds because $xgx^{-1} = c \iff g = x^{-1}cx$. Hence $C(x^{-1}ax) = x^{-1}C(a)x$.
So conjugate elements have conjugate centralizers. In particular, for a finite group, conjugate elements have centralizers of the same order (and so conjugacy classes have well-defined sizes $[G : C(a)]$).

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.18 - The permutations preserving a finite subset form a subgroup
problems.problem: If $S$ is a nonempty set and $X \subset S$, show that $T(X) = \{ f \in A(S) \mid f(X) \subset X \}$ is a subgroup of $A(S)$ if $X$ is finite. (Here $A(S)$ is the group of all bijections of $S$ onto itself.)
problems.hint: • Closure under composition is easy. For inverses, show that $f(X) \subset X$ forces $f(X) = X$ when $X$ is finite.
problems.solution:
Identity. The identity map $i$ satisfies $i(X) = X$, so $i \in T(X)$.
Products. If $f, g \in T(X)$, then $(f \circ g)(X) = f(g(X)) \subset f(X) \subset X$, so $f \circ g \in T(X)$.
Inverses. Let $f \in T(X)$. The restriction $f|_X : X \to X$ is one-to-one (as $f$ is), and $X$ is finite, so $f|_X$ is also onto: $f(X) = X$. (A one-to-one map from a finite set to itself is onto.) Applying $f^{-1}$, we get $X = f^{-1}(X)$, so $f^{-1}(X) \subset X$ and $f^{-1} \in T(X)$.
Hence $T(X)$ is a subgroup of $A(S)$. (The criterion "a nonempty finite subset closed under products is a subgroup" cannot be used here, since $T(X)$ itself may be infinite; it is the finiteness of $X$ that matters. Problem 25 shows it is really needed.)

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.19 - If $A$, $B$ are subgroups of an abelian group, then $AB$ is a subgroup
problems.problem: If $A$, $B$ are subgroups of an abelian group $G$, let $AB = \{ ab \mid a \in A, b \in B \}$. Prove that $AB$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • Use commutativity to rearrange $(a_1 b_1)(a_2 b_2)$ and $(ab)^{-1}$.
problems.solution:
$e = ee \in AB$. Let $a_1 b_1, a_2 b_2 \in AB$. Since $G$ is abelian, \[ (a_1 b_1)(a_2 b_2) = (a_1 a_2)(b_1 b_2) \in AB, \] as $a_1 a_2 \in A$ and $b_1 b_2 \in B$. Also \[ (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1} a^{-1} = a^{-1} b^{-1} \in AB. \] So $AB$ is a subgroup of $G$.
Only part of the commutativity was used: it suffices that elements of $A$ commute with elements of $B$, or more generally that $AB = BA$. Problem 20 shows that some such hypothesis is needed.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.20 - Two subgroups $A$, $B$ of $S_3$ for which $AB$ is not a subgroup
problems.problem: Give an example of a group $G$ and two subgroups $A$, $B$ of $G$ such that $AB$ is not a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • Try $G = S_3$ with $A$ and $B$ generated by two different transpositions.
problems.solution:
Let $G = S_3$, $A = \{ e, (1\ 2) \}$ and $B = \{ e, (1\ 3) \}$. Composing permutations from right to left, \[ (1\ 2)(1\ 3) = (1\ 3\ 2), \qquad (1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2\ 3). \] So \[ AB = \{ e,\ (1\ 2),\ (1\ 3),\ (1\ 3\ 2) \}. \]
$AB$ is not closed under multiplication: $(1\ 3)$ and $(1\ 2)$ are in $AB$, but their product $(1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2\ 3) \notin AB$. Hence $AB$ is not a subgroup of $S_3$. (Alternatively: $AB$ has $4$ elements, and $4$ does not divide $6$, so by Lagrange's theorem it cannot be a subgroup.)

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.21 - If $b^{-1}Ab \subset A$ for all $b \in B$, then $AB$ is a subgroup
problems.problem: If $A$, $B$ are subgroups of $G$ such that $b^{-1}Ab \subset A$ for all $b \in B$, show that $AB$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • Rewrite $b_1 a_2$ as $(b_1 a_2 b_1^{-1})\, b_1$, and $b^{-1}a^{-1}$ as $(b^{-1}a^{-1}b)\, b^{-1}$.
problems.solution:
Clearly $e = ee \in AB$.
Products. Let $a_1 b_1, a_2 b_2 \in AB$. Since $b_1^{-1} \in B$, the hypothesis (applied to $b = b_1^{-1}$) gives $b_1 a_2 b_1^{-1} = (b_1^{-1})^{-1} a_2\, b_1^{-1} \in A$. Hence \[ (a_1 b_1)(a_2 b_2) = a_1 (b_1 a_2 b_1^{-1})\, b_1 b_2 = \big( a_1\, (b_1 a_2 b_1^{-1}) \big) (b_1 b_2) \in AB. \]
Inverses. For $ab \in AB$, $b^{-1} a^{-1} b \in A$ by hypothesis, so \[ (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1} a^{-1} = (b^{-1} a^{-1} b)\, b^{-1} \in AB. \] Hence $AB$ is a subgroup. This generalizes Problem 19, and applies in particular when $A$ is normal in $G$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.22 - In an abelian group, $\vert AB \vert = mn$ when $\vert A \vert = m$, $\vert B \vert = n$ are coprime
problems.problem: If $A$ and $B$ are finite subgroups, of orders $m$ and $n$, respectively, of the abelian group $G$, prove that $AB$ is a subgroup of order $mn$ if $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime.
problems.hint:
• $AB$ is a subgroup by Problem 19. The map $A \times B \to AB$, $(a, b) \mapsto ab$, is onto; show it is one-to-one using $A \cap B$.
  • The order of $A \cap B$ divides both $m$ and $n$ (Lagrange's theorem).
problems.solution:
By Problem 19, $AB$ is a subgroup. Consider the map $\phi : A \times B \to AB$, $\phi(a, b) = ab$. It is onto by definition of $AB$, so $\vert AB \vert \leq mn$, with equality if and only if $\phi$ is one-to-one.
$A \cap B$ is a subgroup of both $A$ and $B$, so by Lagrange's theorem its order divides $m$ and $n$, hence divides $\gcd(m, n) = 1$. Thus $A \cap B = (e)$.
Now if $ab = a'b'$, then $a'^{-1} a = b' b^{-1}$ lies in $A \cap B = (e)$, so $a = a'$ and $b = b'$. Hence $\phi$ is one-to-one and $\vert AB \vert = mn$. (For example, in $\mathbb{Z}_6$ the subgroups $\{ 0, 3 \}$ and $\{ 0, 2, 4 \}$ give $AB = \mathbb{Z}_6$, of order $2 \cdot 3$.)

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.23 - The order of $AB$ when the orders are not relatively prime
problems.problem: What is the order of $AB$ in Problem 22 if $m$ and $n$ are not relatively prime?
problems.hint: • Count how many pairs $(a, b) \in A \times B$ give the same product $ab$.
problems.solution:
Answer: \[ \vert AB \vert = \frac{mn}{\vert A \cap B \vert}. \]
Consider again $\phi : A \times B \to AB$, $\phi(a, b) = ab$. Fix a product $ab$. For each $c \in A \cap B$ the pair $(ac, c^{-1}b)$ lies in $A \times B$ and has the same product. Conversely, if $a'b' = ab$, then $c = a^{-1}a' = b b'^{-1}$ lies in $A \cap B$, and $(a', b') = (ac, c^{-1}b)$. Different $c$ give different pairs. So each element of $AB$ has exactly $\vert A \cap B \vert$ preimages, and \[ mn = \vert A \times B \vert = \vert AB \vert \cdot \vert A \cap B \vert. \]
So the order is not determined by $m$ and $n$ alone. Since $\vert A \cap B \vert$ divides $\gcd(m, n)$, we always have $\operatorname{lcm}(m, n) \leq \vert AB \vert \leq mn$. For example, in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ with $A = \langle 2 \rangle$ (order $6$) and $B = \langle 3 \rangle$ (order $4$): $A \cap B = \langle 6 \rangle$ has order $2$ and $AB = \mathbb{Z}_{12}$ has order $\frac{24}{2} = 12$. (The counting argument does not use commutativity, so the formula holds for the set $AB$ in any group.)

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.24 - The intersection of all conjugates of $H$ is a normal subgroup
problems.problem: If $H$ is a subgroup of $G$, let $N = \bigcap_{x \in G} x^{-1}Hx$. Prove that $N$ is a subgroup of $G$ such that $y^{-1}Ny = N$ for every $y \in G$.
problems.hint: • Each $x^{-1}Hx$ is a subgroup. For the second part, $y^{-1}(x^{-1}Hx)y = (xy)^{-1}H(xy)$, and $xy$ runs over all of $G$ as $x$ does.
problems.solution:
Each conjugate is a subgroup. $e = x^{-1}ex \in x^{-1}Hx$; $(x^{-1}h_1x)(x^{-1}h_2x) = x^{-1}h_1h_2x$; $(x^{-1}hx)^{-1} = x^{-1}h^{-1}x$. An intersection of subgroups is a subgroup, so $N$ is a subgroup of $G$.
$N$ is normal. Fix $y \in G$. Since $g \mapsto y^{-1}gy$ is a bijection of $G$, it maps intersections to intersections: \[ y^{-1}Ny = \bigcap_{x \in G} y^{-1}(x^{-1}Hx)y = \bigcap_{x \in G} (xy)^{-1}H(xy) = \bigcap_{z \in G} z^{-1}Hz = N, \] because as $x$ runs over $G$, so does $z = xy$.
$N$ is the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$ (the "core" of $H$): it is contained in $H = e^{-1}He$, and any normal subgroup $K \subseteq H$ satisfies $K = x^{-1}Kx \subseteq x^{-1}Hx$ for all $x$, so $K \subseteq N$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.25 - For an infinite subset $X$, $T(X)$ need not be a subgroup
problems.problem: Let $S$, $X$, $T(X)$ be as in Problem 18 (but $X$ no longer finite). Give an example of a set $S$ and an infinite subset $X$ such that $T(X)$ is not a subgroup of $A(S)$.
problems.hint: • Take $S = \mathbb{Z}$, $X = \{ 1, 2, 3, \dots \}$ and the shift $f(n) = n + 1$.
problems.solution:
Let $S = \mathbb{Z}$, $X = \{ 1, 2, 3, \dots \}$, and $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$, $f(n) = n + 1$. Then $f$ is a bijection, so $f \in A(S)$, and \[ f(X) = \{ 2, 3, 4, \dots \} \subset X, \] so $f \in T(X)$.
But $f^{-1}(n) = n - 1$, and $f^{-1}(1) = 0 \notin X$, so $f^{-1}(X) \not\subset X$ and $f^{-1} \notin T(X)$. Hence $T(X)$ is not closed under inverses, and is not a subgroup of $A(S)$. (It is closed under composition and contains the identity: it is a "submonoid".)
The proof of Problem 18 breaks down exactly here: $f|_X : X \to X$ is one-to-one but not onto, which is possible only because $X$ is infinite.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.26 - Two right cosets are either equal or disjoint
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a group, $H$ a subgroup of $G$. Let $Hx = \{ hx \mid h \in H \}$. Show that, given $a, b \in G$, then $Ha = Hb$ or $Ha \cap Hb = \varnothing$.
problems.hint: • If $x \in Ha \cap Hb$, write $x = h_1 a = h_2 b$ and use $Hh = H$ for $h \in H$.
problems.solution:
First, $Hh = H$ for every $h \in H$: $Hh \subseteq H$ by closure, and any $k \in H$ equals $(kh^{-1})h \in Hh$.
Suppose $Ha \cap Hb \neq \varnothing$, say $x = h_1 a = h_2 b$ with $h_1, h_2 \in H$. Then $a = h_1^{-1} h_2\, b$, and \[ Ha = H(h_1^{-1}h_2)\, b = Hb, \] because $h_1^{-1}h_2 \in H$. So two right cosets are either equal or disjoint.
Since every $a \in G$ lies in its own coset $Ha$, the right cosets of $H$ partition $G$.

problems.title: If G/Z(G) is cyclic, then G is abelian
problems.problem:
<ul class="leading-relaxed lg:text-lg md:text-base text-justify">
Let $G$ be a group which has a normal subgroup $N$ of order $2$. If $G /N$ is cyclic, then $G$ is abelian.
problems.solution:
Given that $N$ is a normal subgroup of order $2$. Let $N = \{ e,h \} $. For any $g\in G$, we have \[ ghg^{-1} = h \implies gh = hg. \] Thus $h$ commutes with every element of $G$ and hence, $N = Z(G)$, where $Z(G)$ denotes the centre of $G$.

Now let us prove a general statement. If $G/Z(G)$ is cyclic, then $G$ is abelian. Since $G/Z(G)$ is cyclic, there exists $g\in G$ such that $\left\langle g Z(G) \right\rangle = G / Z(G)$. For any $x \in G$, there exists $k\in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $x Z(G) = g^k Z(G)$. Thus, \[ x Z(G) = g^k Z(G) \implies g^{-k} x \in Z(G) \implies x = g^k z \text{ for some $z \in Z(G)$}. \] In other words, given any element $x \in G$ there exists $z \in Z(G)$ and $k\in \mathbb{Z} $ such that $x = g^k z$. For any $x_1, x_2 \in G$, let $x_1 = g^{k_1}z_1$ and $x_2 = g^{k_2}z_2$ for some $z_1,z_2 \in Z(G)$ and $k_1, k_2 \in \mathbb{Z} $. Thus, \begin{align*} x_1 x_2 & = \left( g^{k_1}z_1 \right) \left( g^{k_2} z_2 \right) = \left( g^{k_2} z_2 \right) \left( g^{k_1} z_1 \right) = x_2 x_1. \end{align*} Thus, $G$ is abelian.

problems.title: Every nonzero element of $\mathbb{Z} _n$ is either a unit or a zero divisor, but not both
problems.problem: Prove that for every nonzero element $\mathbb{Z} _n$ is either a unit or a zero divisor, but not both.
problems.solution:
Let $a$ be a nonzero element of $\mathbb{Z} _n$. Suppose that $a$ is a unit. We claim that $a$ can not be a zero divisor. If $a$ is a zero divisor, then there exists a nonzero $b \in \mathbb{Z} _n$ such that \[ a b = 0 \implies a^{-1} \left( a b \right) = 0 \implies b = 0, \] a contradiction. Thus, $a$ is not a zero divisor.
On the other hand, if $a$ is a zero divisor, then $a$ can not be a unit. If not, then there exists $c \in \mathbb{Z} _n$ such that $ac = 1$. Since $a$ is a zero divisor, there exists a nonzero element $d\in \mathbb{Z} _n$ such that $ad = 0$. We have \[ ad = 0 \implies c (ad) = 0 \implies d = 0, \] a contradiction. Thus, $a$ can not be a unit.

problems.title: $[\mathbb{F} : \mathbb{Q} ]$ is infinite.
problems.problem: Let $\mathbb{F}$ be the field of complex numbers which are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q} $. Then show that $[\mathbb{F} : \mathbb{Q} ]$ is infinite.
problems.solution: We need to show that $[\mathbb{F} : \mathbb{Q} ]$ is infinite. Let us assume that it is finite and $[\mathbb{F} : \mathbb{Q} ] = n$. Choose a prime number $p$ such that $p > n + 2$. Then the polynomial \[ x^p - 1 = (x - 1) \left( x^{p-1} + \dots + x + 1 \right) \implies \frac{x^p - 1}{x - 1} = x^{p-1} + \dots + x + 1. \] By Eisenstein criteria (for irreducibility of a polynomial), this is an irreducible polynomial as the polynomial \begin{align*} \frac{(x + 1)^p - 1}{(x + 1) - 1} = x^{p-1} + p x^{p-2} + \dots p x + p \end{align*} is irreducible. Since $\mathbb{F} $ is algebraic, every $p^{\text{th} }$ root of unity is in $\mathbb{F} $. Hence for the prime $p$, there exists an element $\alpha _p$ algebraic over $\mathbb{Q} $ and $[\mathbb{Q} (\alpha _p): \mathbb{Q} ] \geq p-1$. Thus, \begin{align*} n = [\mathbb{F} : Q] \geq [\mathbb{Q} (\alpha _p) : \mathbb{Q} ] \geq p-1 > n + 1, \end{align*} a contradiction. Thus, $[\mathbb{F} : \mathbb{Q} ]$ is infinite.

problems.title: Multiplicities of zeros of a polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}_5$
problems.problem:
Consider $\mathbb{Z} _5$ as a field modulo $5$ and let \[ f(x) = x^5 + 4x^4 + 4x^3 + 4x^2 + x + 1. \] Then the zero of $f(x)$ over $\mathbb{Z} _5$ are $1$ and $3$ with respective multiplicity
    • $1$ and $4$
    • $2$ and $3$
    • $2$ and $2$
    • $1$ and $2$
problems.solution: We recall that if $x = a$ is a root of $f(x)$ with multiplicity $m$, then \[ f(x) = (x-a)^m g(x),\quad g(a)\neq 0. \] This implies $f(a) = 0$ and $f^{(i)}(a) = 0$ for $1\leq i\leq m-1$ and $f^{(m)}(a) \neq 0$. Here we have $f(1) = 0 = f(3)$. Consider \begin{align*} f'(x) & = 5x^4 + 16x^3 + 12x^2 + 8x + 1 \\ & \equiv \left(x^3 + 2x^2 + 3x + 1\right) \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 5) \\ \implies f'(1) & = (1 + 2 + 3 + 1) \equiv 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 5) \\ \implies f'(3) & = (27 + 18 + 9 + 1) \equiv 0 (\mathrm{mod}\ 5). \end{align*} Thus, the multiplicity of $x= 1$ is $1$. Similarly, \begin{align*} f''(x) & = 3x^2 + 4x + 3 \\ \implies f''(3) & = 27 + 12 + 3 \equiv 42 (\mathrm{mod}\ 5) \equiv 2 (\mathrm{mod}\ 5). \end{align*} Thus, the multiplicity of $5$ is $2$. Therefore the correct answer is Option D.

problems.title: Number of group homomorphisms from S_3 to Z_3 and from Z_3 to S_3
problems.problem:
Let $S_3$ denotes the group of permutation on three letters (symmetric group). Find the number of group homomorphisms
    • from $S_3$ to $\mathbb{Z} _3 \left( \cong \mathbb{Z} / 3\mathbb{Z} \right) $,
    • from $\mathbb{Z} _3$ to $S_3$.
problems.solution:
We need to find number of group homomorphisms between $S_3$ and $\mathbb{Z} _3$ and vice versa. let us write \[ S_3 = \{ e, \sigma = (1,2,3), \sigma ^2, \tau = (1,2), \sigma \tau, \sigma ^2\tau\}. \]
  • Let $f: S_3 \to \mathbb{Z} _3$ be a homomorphism. If $f$ is not trivial, then it must be surjective. Therefore, from the first isomorphism theorem we have \[ S_3 / \ker f \cong \mathbb{Z} _3 \implies \left\vert S^3 /\ker f \right\vert = \left\vert \mathbb{Z} _3 \right\vert \implies \left\vert \ker f \right\vert = 2. \] We also know that $\ker f$ is normal subgroup. Thus if $f$ is nontrivial, then $\ker f$ is of order $2$ normal subgroup of $S_3$. From here we can can get contradiction in two ways.
    • If $N \leqslant G$ is a normal subgroup of order $2$ and $G / N$ is cyclic, then $G$ is abelian. (See problem for 24th April 2024.)
    • Look at the order $2$ subgroups in $S_3$. Let $N = \{ e, \tau \} $. Consider \begin{align*} \sigma N \sigma ^{-1} = \{ e, \sigma \tau \sigma ^{-1} \} = \{ e, \sigma ^2\tau \} \neq N. \end{align*} Similarly, if you take the other two subgroups, then also it is easy to see that they are not normal. Therefore, there does not exist any normal subgroup of order $2$.
    Therefore, $\ker f$ can not be of order $2$ and hence, $f$ must be the trivial homomorphism. Thus, there is only one homomorphism from $S_3$ to $\mathbb{Z} _3$.
  • Now we need to find the number of homomorphisms from $\mathbb{Z} _3$ to $S_3$. Since $\mathbb{Z} _3$ is cyclic, any homomorphism is determined by its generator. That is, if $f : \mathbb{Z} _3 \to S_3$ is a homomorphism, then it is determined by $f(1)$. If $o(g)$ denotes the order of $g$, then we know that $o(f(1))$ must divide $o(1) = 3$. This implies $o(f(1))$ is either $1$ or $3$. Look at the following possibilities. \begin{align*} & o(f(1)) = 1 \implies f(1) = e \implies f \text{ is trivial}. \\ & o(f(1)) = 3 \implies f(1) \in \{\sigma ,\sigma ^2\}. \end{align*} Thus, the total number of homomorphisms are $3$. (The number of nontrivial homomorphisms are precisely the order $3$ elements in $S_3$.)

problems.title: Z[i]/(a+ ib) isomorphic to Z/(a^2 + b^2)Z if gcd(a,b) = 1
problems.problem:
Let $a,b \in \mathbb{Z} $ such that $\gcd (a,b) = 1$. Let
\[
    \mathbb{Z} [i] = \left\{ x + \iota y : x,y \in \mathbb{Z}  \right\}.
\]
Show that
\[
    \frac{\mathbb{Z}[i]}{\left\langle a + \iota b \right\rangle} \cong \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{\left\langle a^2 + b^2 \right\rangle} = \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{(a^2 + b^2)\mathbb{Z} }.
\]
problems.solution:
Define a map \[ f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \frac{\mathbb{Z} [\iota ]}{\left\langle a + \iota b \right\rangle },\quad m \mapsto [m] = m + \left\langle a + \iota b \right\rangle. \] It is clear that the map is a homomorphism. We will show that the above map is surjective with kernel being $\left\langle a^2 + b^2 \right\rangle $.
  • The map $f$ is surjective. Since $\gcd (a,b) = 1$, there exists $p,q\in \mathbb{Z} $ such that $ap + bq = 1$. Consider \begin{align*} (a + \iota b)(q + \iota p) & = (aq - bp) + \iota (ap + bq) = aq - bp + \iota. \end{align*} This implies, \begin{align*} [a + \iota b] = [aq - bp + \iota] \implies [\iota] = [bp - aq] \in \frac{\mathbb{Z} [\iota ]}{\left\langle a+\iota b \right\rangle }. \end{align*} Let us denote $bp - aq$ by $A$. Since, $A \in \mathbb{Z} $, for any $x + \iota y \in \mathbb{Z} [\iota ]$, we have \begin{align*} f(x + Ay) = x + Ay + \left\langle a + \iota b \right\rangle = x + \iota y + \left\langle a + \iota b \right\rangle . \end{align*} This shows that $f$ is surjective.
  • We now claim that $\ker f $ is generated by $a^2 + b^2$. \begin{align*} m \in \ker f & \iff f(m) = 0 \iff m \in a + \iota b \iff (a + \iota b) \mid m \\ & \iff \frac{m}{a + \iota b} \in \mathbb{Z} \iff \frac{m}{a + \iota b}\times \frac{a - \iota b}{a - \iota b} \in \mathbb{Z} \\ & \iff \frac{m(a - \iota b)}{a^2 + b^2} \in \mathbb{Z} \iff (a^2 + b^2) \mid ma, mb \\ & \iff (a^2 + b^2) \mid \gcd (ma, mb) \\ & \iff (a^2 + b^2) \mid m. \end{align*} Thus, $\ker f = \left\langle a^2 + b^2 \right\rangle $.
Hence, from the first isomorphism theorem, we conclude that \[ \textcolor{teal}{\boxed{ \frac{\mathbb{Z}[i]}{\left\langle a + \iota b \right\rangle} \cong \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{\left\langle a^2 + b^2 \right\rangle} = \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{(a^2 + b^2)\mathbb{Z} } }} \]

problems.title: The number of elements in $GL_{2}\left( \mathbb{F} _3 \right)$
problems.problem: Let $\mathbb{F}_3$ be the field with exactly $3$ elements. The number of elements in $GL_{2}\left( \mathbb{F} _3 \right)$ is equal to ______________.

problems.title: Group homomorphism between Z/mZ to Z/nZ
problems.problem:
Let $m,n$ be two positive integers such that $n$ divides $m$.
  • Prove that the map \[ \varphi : \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} / n\mathbb{Z},\ a + m\mathbb{Z} \mapsto a + n\mathbb{Z} \] is a well-defined surjective group homomorphism.
  • Determine the group structure of the kernel of $\varphi $.
problems.solution:
We are given that $n \mid m$.
  • Let us prove that the map is well defined. That is, if $a + m\mathbb{Z} = b + m\mathbb{Z} $, then $a+n\mathbb{Z} = b + n\mathbb{Z} $. Equivalently, if $m \mid (b-a)$ then $n \mid (b-a)$. Since \[ m \mid (b-a) \text{ and } n \mid m \implies n \mid (b-a). \] Thus, the map is well defined.
    We now prove that $\varphi $ is a homomorphism. Before that we recall that the operation on the quotient group $\mathbb{Z} /n \mathbb{Z} $ is \[ (a + n\mathbb{Z}) + (b + n\mathbb{Z}) = (a + b) + n\mathbb{Z} . \] Consider \begin{align*} \varphi \left( (a + m\mathbb{Z}) + (b + m\mathbb{Z} ) \right) & = \varphi \left( (a+b) + m \mathbb{Z} \right) \\ & = (a + b) + n\mathbb{Z} \\ & = (a + n\mathbb{Z} ) + (b + n\mathbb{Z} ) \\ & = \varphi (a + m\mathbb{Z} ) + \varphi (b + m\mathbb{Z} ). \end{align*} Thus, the map is well defined.
    Now let us prove that $\varphi $ is surjective. Let $y + n\mathbb{Z} \in \mathbb{Z} /n\mathbb{Z} $. Then $y + m\mathbb{Z} \in \mathbb{Z} /m\mathbb{Z} $ and \[ \varphi (y + m\mathbb{Z} ) = y + n\mathbb{Z} . \]
  • Let us first find the kernel of the homomorphism. \begin{align*} \ker \varphi & = \left\{ a + m\mathbb{Z} : \varphi (a + m\mathbb{Z} ) = 0 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ a + m\mathbb{Z} : a + n \mathbb{Z} = 0 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ a + m \mathbb{Z} : n \mid a \right\}. \end{align*} Let us simplify the kernel that we obtained. If $a + m\mathbb{Z} \in \ker \varphi $, then $n \mid a$, that is, $a = nk$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z} $. So, $a + m\mathbb{Z} = nk + m\mathbb{Z}$. As $n \mid m$, we can also write $m = nl$ for some $l \in \mathbb{Z} $. Thus we obtained \[ a + m\mathbb{Z} = nk + nl \mathbb{Z} . \] Thus, \[ \ker \varphi = \left\{ nk + nl \mathbb{Z} : k = 0,1,\dots, l-1 \right\}. \] So, the order of $\ker \varphi $ is $l$ and being a subgroup of a cyclic group it must be cyclic. Thus, \[ \ker \varphi \cong \mathbb{Z} /l\mathbb{Z} . \]

problems.title: Prove that $o(ab) = o(a0 o(b)$ if the orders are coprime and ab = ba
problems.problem:
Let $G$ be a group and $a , b \in G$ be such that
\[
    ab = ba \text{ and } \gcd (o(a), o(b)) = 1,
\]
where $o(a)$ denotes the order of $a$. Then prove that $o(ab) = o(a) o(b)$.
problems.solution:
Let us assume that $o(a) = m$, $o(b) = n$ and $o(ab) = k$. Then, \[ a^m = e = b^n = (ab)^k. \] Since $a$ and $b$ commutes, we have \begin{align*} (ab)^k = a^k b^k & \implies a^k b^k = e \\ & \implies a^k = b^{-k} \\ & \implies a^{nk} = b^{-nk} = e \\ & \implies m \mid nk \\ & \implies m \mid k \quad (\text{ since } \gcd (m,n) = 1). \end{align*}
Similarly, \begin{align*} b^k = a^{-k} & \implies b^{mk} = a^{-mk} = e \\ & \implies n \mid mk \\ & \implies n \mid k . \end{align*} Since $\gcd (m,n) = 1$ we must have $mn \mid k$.

We also have \begin{align*} (ab)^ {mn} = a^{mn} b^{mn} = e \implies k \mid mn. \end{align*} Since $m,n$ and $k$ are positive integers, we have $mn = k$ and therefore, we proved that \[ o(ab) = o(a) o(b). \]

problems.title: Units in the matrix ring over quaternions
problems.solution:
Let \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} a + \iota b & c + \iota d \\ -c + \iota d & a - \iota b \\ \end{bmatrix} \] be a unit in $H$. Therefore, $A^{-1} \in H$. Since $A^{-1} $ exists, the determinant of $A$ must be nonzero, that is, $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \neq 0$. Note that \[ A^{-1} = \frac{1}{a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2} \begin{bmatrix} a - \iota b & -c - \iota d \\ c - \iota d & a + \iota b \\ \end{bmatrix} \in H. \]
So $A^{-1} \in H \iff a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \in \mathbb{Z} $. Since $a,b,c,d\in \mathbb{Z} $, the following are the possibilities. \begin{align*} a = \pm 1,\ b = c = d = 0 \\ b = \pm 1,\ a = c = d = 0 \\ c = \pm 1,\ a = b = d = 0 \\ d = \pm 1,\ a = b = c = 0. \end{align*} Therefore, the units in $H$ are \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} \pm 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \pm 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} \pm \iota & 0 \\ 0 & \mp \iota \\ \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \pm 1 \\ \mp 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \pm \iota \\ \pm \iota & 0\\ \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

problems.title: Polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z} _5 [x]$ over $\mathbb{Z} _5$ is an integral domain
problems.problem: Prove that the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z} _5 [x]$ over $\mathbb{Z} _5$ is an integral domain.
problems.solution: Since $\mathbb{Z} _5$ is a commutative ring, $\mathbb{Z} _5[x]$ is also a commutative ring. We just need to show that it does not have a zero divisor. That is, if $p(x), q(x) \in \mathbb{Z} _5[x]$ such that \[ p(x) q(x) = 0 \implies p(x) = 0 \text{ or } q(x) = 0. \] We will show that if $p(x) \neq 0$ and $q(x) \neq 0$, then $p(x) q(x) \neq 0$. Let \begin{align*} & p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \dots + a_m x^m, a_i \in \mathbb{Z} _5 \text{ and } a_m \neq 0 \\ & q(x) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2 + \dots + b_n x^n, b_i \in \mathbb{Z} _5 \text{ and } b_n \neq 0. \end{align*} Then \begin{align*} p(x) q(x) = a_0 b_0 + \dots + a_m b_n x^{m + n}. \end{align*} Since $a_m , b_n \in \mathbb{Z} _5$, $a_m, b_n$ both are nonzero and $\mathbb{Z} _5$ is an integral domain (it is a filed), so $a_m b_n \neq 0$. Thus, $p(x) q(x) \neq 0$. Hence, $\mathbb{Z} _5[x]$ is an integral domain.

problems.title: The number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $2^2\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^4$
problems.problem: The number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $2^2\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^4$ is _______________.
problems.solution:
Before proceeding for a solution to the problem, let us see the number of non-isomorphic abelian group of order $p^4$, where $p$ is a prime. We consider all partitions of $4$. Each partition will give an abelian group of order $p^5$. We have \begin{align*} & 4 & & \mathbb{Z} _{p^4} \\ & 3 + 1 & & \mathbb{Z} _{p^3} \oplus \mathbb{Z} _p \\ & 2 + 2 & & \mathbb{Z} _{p^2} \oplus \mathbb{Z} _{p^2} \\ & 2 + 1 + 1 & & \mathbb{Z} _{p^2} \oplus \mathbb{Z} _{p} \oplus \mathbb{Z} _{p} \\ & 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 & & \mathbb{Z} _{p} \oplus \mathbb{Z} _{p} \oplus \mathbb{Z} _{p} \mathbb{Z} _{p} . \end{align*} So there are $5$ non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $p^4$.
In order to determine the number of non-isomorphic groups of order $2^2 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 5^4$, we consider the partition of each powers. So we have
  • The number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $2^2$ is parton of $2$, that is, $2$.
  • The number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $3^3$ is parton of $3$, that is, $3$.
  • The number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $5^4$ is parton of $4$, that is, $5$.
Therefore, total number of non-isomorphic abelian group of order $2^2\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^4$ is $30$.

problems.title: Find all idempotent elements of the ring $Z_5[i]$
problems.problem:
Find all idempotent elements of the ring
\[
    \mathbb{Z} _5[\iota ] = \left\{ a + b \iota : a,b \in \mathbb{Z} _5 \right\}.
\]
problems.solution:
We need to find all idempotent elements in $\mathbb{Z} _5[\iota ]$. Recall that $a$ is said to be idempotent if $a^2 = a$.
Let $I(R)$ denote the set of all idempotent elements in $R$. Then, \begin{equation}\label{eq:17July2024-1} I\left( \mathbb{Z} _5[\iota ] \right) = \left\{ a + b \iota \in \mathbb{Z} _5 [\iota ] : (a + b \iota )^2 = a + b \iota \right\}. \end{equation} Note that if $a,b\in \mathbb{Z} _5$ with \begin{align*} (a + b \iota )^2 = (a + b \iota ) & \implies a^2 - b^2 + 2ab \iota = a + b \iota \\ & \implies (a^2 + b^2 -a) + (2a - 1)b \equiv 0 \text{ mod } 5\\ & \implies a^2 - b^2 - a \equiv 0 \text{ mod } 5 \\ & \kern 1cm \text{ and } (2a - 1)b \equiv 0 \text{ mod } 5. \end{align*} If $(2a - 1) b \equiv 0 \text{ mod } 5$, then as $\mathbb{Z} _5$ is an integral domain, \begin{align*} 2a - 1 = 0 \text{ or } b = 0 \implies a = 3 \text{ or } b = 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{Z} _5 . \end{align*} If $a \equiv 3 \text{ mod } 5$, then \begin{align*} a^2 - b^2 -a =0 & \implies 9 - b^2 - 3 = 0 \\ & \implies 6 - b^2 = 0 \\ & \implies b^2 = 1 \\ & \implies b = 1, 4. \end{align*} If $b \equiv 0 \text{ mod } 5$, then \begin{align*} a^2 - b^2 - a = 0 \implies a ^2 = a \implies a = 1. \end{align*} Thus, \[ I\left( \mathbb{Z} _5 [\iota ] \right) = \left\{ 1, 3 + \iota , 3 + 4 \iota \right\} . \]

problems.title: Order of a group G for which Z_10 and Z_15 are homeomorphic images
problems.problem: Let $\mathbb{Z} _{10}$ and $\mathbb{Z} _{15}$ are homomorphic images of a group $G$. What can be concluded about the order of $G$. Also, generalize this.
problems.solution:
Let $\phi : G \to \mathbb{Z} _{10}$ be $\psi : G \to \mathbb{Z} _{15}$ be surjective homomorphisms. From the first isomorphism theorem, \[ \frac{G}{\ker \phi } \cong \mathbb{Z} _{10} \quad \text{ and }\quad \frac{G}{\ker \psi } \cong \mathbb{Z} _{15}. \] Therefore, \[ \left\vert \frac{G}{\ker \phi } \right\vert = 10 \quad \text{ and } \quad \left\vert \frac{G}{\ker \psi } \right\vert = 15, \] which implies \begin{align*} \frac{\vert G \vert }{10} = \vert \ker \phi \vert \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{\vert G \vert }{15} = \vert \ker \psi \vert. \end{align*} Hence, \[ 10 \mid \vert G \vert \text{ and } 15 \mid \vert G \vert \implies \mathrm{lcm} (10,15) = 30 \mid \vert G \vert \]
In general, if $\mathbb{Z} _m$ and $\mathbb{Z} _n$ are homomorphic images of $G$, then $\mathrm{lcm}(m,n) $ must divide the order of $G$. It can be further generalize as if $H_1$ and $H_2$ are two groups of order $m$ and $n$ are homomorphic images of $G$, then $\mathrm{lcm}(m,n) $ must divide order of $G$.

problems.title: How many generators does a cyclic group of order $36$ have?
problems.problem:
How many generators does a cyclic group of order $36$ have?
  • $6$
  • $12$
  • $18$
  • $24$
problems.solution:
Let us see a general result along the same line. Let $G$ be a cyclic group of order $n$. Let $g$ be a generator of $G$. Then \[ o\left( g^k \right) = \frac{n}{\gcd (n,k)}. \] Therefore, $g^k$ will be another generator of $G$ if $o\left( g^k \right) = n$, that is $\gcd (n,k) = 1$. Therefore, the number of generators of a cyclic group of order $n$ is \[ \#\left\{ k \in \mathbb{N} : \gcd (n,k) = 1, \text{ and } k \leq n \right\} = \phi (n), \] where $\phi$ is the Euler-phi function.
The number of generators of a cyclic group of order $36$ is \[ \phi (36) = \phi (2^2 \times 3^2) = \phi (2^2) \times \phi (3^2) = 2 \times 6 = 12. \]

problems.title: Degree of $Q(\sqrt{3}, \iota, \omega)$ over $Q$
problems.problem: Let $\omega $ be a primitive complex cube root of unity and $\iota = \sqrt{-1} $. Then the degree of the field extension $\mathbb{Q} (\iota , \sqrt{3},\omega  )$ over $\mathbb{Q} $ (the field of rational numbers) is _______________.
problems.solution:
Note that \[ \omega = \frac{1-\sqrt{3}\iota}{2} \implies \omega \in \mathbb{Q} (\iota ,\sqrt{3} ). \] Therefore, \[ \mathbb{Q} (\iota ,\sqrt{3}, \omega ) = \mathbb{Q} (\iota , \sqrt{3} ). \] So, we need to determine the degree of the field extension $\mathbb{Q} (\iota ,\sqrt{3} )$. Since, $\iota \notin \mathbb{Q} (\sqrt{3} )$ and $\sqrt{3} \notin \mathbb{Q} (\iota )$, the polynomial \[ (x^2 + 1)(x^2 -\sqrt{3} ) \] is the minimal polynomial containing $\iota $ and $\sqrt{3} $. Therefore, the degree of the extension field will be the degree of the minimal polynomial, which is $4$.
This can also be viewed as \begin{align*} \deg \left( Q(\iota , \sqrt{3} , \omega ) \right) & = \deg \left( \mathbb{Q} (\iota ,\sqrt{3} ) \right) \\ & = \left[ \mathbb{Q} (\iota ,\sqrt{3} ): \mathbb{Q} \right] \\ & = \left[ \mathbb{Q} (\iota ,\sqrt{3} ): \mathbb{Q} (\iota ) \right] \left[ \mathbb{Q} (\iota ): \mathbb{Q} \right] \\ & = 2 \times 2 = 4. \end{align*}

problems.title: If $a$ is a unit, then $b$ divides $c$ if and only if $ab$ divides $c$
problems.problem: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $a,b, c \in R$. Suppose that $a$ is a unit. Prove that $b$ divides $c$ if and only if $ab$ divides $c$.
problems.solution:
Given that $a$ is a unit, means we can find $x \in R$ such that $ax = 1 = xa$. Let $b$ divides $c$, that is, there exists $r \in R$ such that \begin{align*} c = br \implies c = 1\cdot br & \implies c = xa br \\ & \implies c = (ab)\cdot (xr). \end{align*} Thus, $ab$ divides $c$.
On the other hand, let $ab$ divides $c$, that is, there exists $q \in R$ such that \begin{align*} c = ab q \implies c = b (aq). \end{align*} Thus, $b$ divides $c$.

problems.title: Show that $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} $ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q} $ and find its degree over $\mathbb{Q} $
problems.problem: In a field $\mathbb{F} $, an element $\alpha $ is said to be algebraic if there exists a polynomial $p(x) \in \mathbb{F} [x]$ such that $p(\alpha ) = 0$. For example, $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3} $ both are algebraic over $\mathbb{R} $ as $x^2 - 2, x^2 - 3 \in \mathbb{R} [x]$. Show that $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} $ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q} $ and find its degree over $\mathbb{Q} $. What is the degree of $\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{3} $ over $\mathbb{Q} $?
problems.solution:
Let $x = \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} $. Then we have \begin{align*} x^2 = 2 + 3 + 2\sqrt{6} & \implies x^2 - 5 = 2\sqrt{6} \\ & \implies (x^2 - 5)^2 = 24 \\ & \implies x^4 -10x^2 + 25 - 24 = 0 \\ & \implies x^4 - 10x^2 + 1 = 0. \end{align*} Since the polynomial $p(x) = x^4 - 10x^2 + 1 \in \mathbb{Q} [x]$, the number $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} $ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q} $.
To determine the degree $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} $ over $\mathbb{Q} $, we observe that the polynomial $x^4 - 10x^2 + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q} $. To see this note that the only possible rational roots are $\pm 1$. Since $p(1)$ and $p(-1)$ are nonzero, the polynomial $p(x)$ does not have a rational root. Also, $p(x)$ cannot be factored as a product of two quadratic polynomials. For that, let \begin{align*} & p(x) = \left( x^2 + ax + b\right) \left( x^2 - ax + b\right) \\ \implies & x^4 +x^2 \left( 2b - a^2 \right) + b^2. \end{align*} Comparing the coefficients, we get \begin{align*} b^2 = 1 \text{ and } 2b - a^2 = -10, \end{align*} the above does not have a solution in $\mathbb{Q} $. Thus, $p(x)$ is irreducible and hence $\left[ \mathbb{Q} \left( \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} : \mathbb{Q} \right) \right] = 4$.
Similarly to determine the degree of $\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{3} $, we observe that if \[ x = \sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{3} \implies x^2 = 6. \] Thus, $x^2 - 6$ is the minimal polynomial (as the polynomial is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q} $) that satisfies $\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{6} $. Hence, $\left[ \mathbb{Q} (\sqrt{6} ) : \mathbb{Q} \right] = 2 $.

problems.title: For an infinite cyclic group there are only two generators
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a cyclic group of infinite order. Let $G = \left\langle a \right\rangle $. Then prove that $a$ and $a^{-1}$ are the only generators of $G$.
problems.solution:
Let $G$ can be generated by $b$, that is, $G = \left\langle b \right\rangle $ for some $b \in G$. Since $b \in G = \left\langle a \right\rangle $, there exists $m \in \mathbb{Z} $ such that $b = a^m$. Since, $a\in G$ so there exists $l \in \mathbb{Z} $ such that $a = b^l$. Thus, \[ b = a^m \implies b^l = a^{ml } \implies a = a^{ml}. \] Since $G$ is of infante order, and $a$ is a generator, the above is possible if and only if $ml = 1$. This means $m,l \in \{ 1, -1 \} $. Therefore, \[ b = a \text{ or } b = a^{-1} . \]
Now it only remains to show that $G = \left\langle a^{-1} \right\rangle $. We will show that $a \in \left\langle a^{-1} \right\rangle, $ which will prove the claim. Since $a = \left( a^{-1} \right)^{-1} $, it is clear that $a \in \left\langle a^{-1} \right\rangle $.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.27 - All right cosets of a finite subgroup $H$ have $o(H)$ elements
problems.problem: If in Problem 26 $H$ is a finite subgroup of $G$, prove that $Ha$ and $Hb$ have the same number of elements. What is this number?
problems.hint: • The map $H \to Ha$, $h \mapsto ha$, is a bijection.
problems.solution:
The map $\phi_a : H \to Ha$, $\phi_a(h) = ha$, is onto by the definition of $Ha$, and one-to-one: $h_1 a = h_2 a$ implies $h_1 = h_2$ by cancellation. So $\vert Ha \vert = \vert H \vert$ for every $a \in G$.
Hence $Ha$ and $Hb$ have the same number of elements, namely $o(H)$, the order of $H$.
Together with Problem 26 this gives Lagrange's theorem: if $G$ is finite, it is a disjoint union of, say, $k$ right cosets, each with $o(H)$ elements, so $o(G) = k \cdot o(H)$ and $o(H)$ divides $o(G)$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.28 - If $M$, $N$ are normal subgroups, then $MN$ is a normal subgroup
problems.problem: Let $M$, $N$ be subgroups of $G$ such that $x^{-1}Mx \subset M$ and $x^{-1}Nx \subset N$ for all $x \in G$. Prove that $MN$ is a subgroup of $G$ and that $x^{-1}(MN)x \subset MN$ for all $x \in G$.
problems.hint: • For the first part apply Problem 21; for the second, $x^{-1}mnx = (x^{-1}mx)(x^{-1}nx)$.
problems.solution:
$MN$ is a subgroup. In particular $n^{-1}Mn \subset M$ for every $n \in N$, so by Problem 21 (with $A = M$, $B = N$), $MN$ is a subgroup of $G$.
$MN$ is normal. For $m \in M$, $n \in N$ and $x \in G$, \[ x^{-1}(mn)x = (x^{-1}mx)(x^{-1}nx) \in MN, \] since $x^{-1}mx \in M$ and $x^{-1}nx \in N$. Hence $x^{-1}(MN)x \subset MN$.
So the product of two normal subgroups is a normal subgroup (and by Problem 29 the inclusion is in fact an equality).

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.29 - If $x^{-1}Mx \subset M$ for all $x$, then $x^{-1}Mx = M$
problems.problem: If $M$ is a subgroup of $G$ such that $x^{-1}Mx \subset M$ for all $x \in G$, prove that actually $x^{-1}Mx = M$.
problems.hint: • Apply the hypothesis to $x^{-1}$ instead of $x$.
problems.solution:
Fix $x \in G$. We already have $x^{-1}Mx \subset M$; we need $M \subset x^{-1}Mx$.
Applying the hypothesis to the element $x^{-1}$ gives $(x^{-1})^{-1} M x^{-1} = xMx^{-1} \subset M$. So for $m \in M$, $xmx^{-1} = m'$ for some $m' \in M$, and then \[ m = x^{-1} m' x \in x^{-1}Mx. \] Hence $M \subset x^{-1}Mx$, and so $x^{-1}Mx = M$.
The point is that the hypothesis is for all $x$. For a single fixed $x$ the inclusion $x^{-1}Mx \subset M$ can be strict in an infinite group (although not in a finite one, where both sides have the same number of elements).

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.30 - Normal subgroups with trivial intersection commute elementwise
problems.problem: If $M$, $N$ are such that $x^{-1}Mx = M$ and $x^{-1}Nx = N$ for all $x \in G$, and if $M \cap N = (e)$, prove that $mn = nm$ for any $m \in M$, $n \in N$. (Hint: Consider the element $m^{-1}n^{-1}mn$.)
problems.hint: • Show that the commutator $m^{-1}n^{-1}mn$ lies in $M$ (group it as $m^{-1}(n^{-1}mn)$) and in $N$ (group it as $(m^{-1}n^{-1}m)\,n$).
problems.solution:
Let $m \in M$, $n \in N$, and $c = m^{-1}n^{-1}mn$.
$c \in M$: $n^{-1}mn \in n^{-1}Mn = M$, so $c = m^{-1}\,(n^{-1}mn)$ is a product of two elements of $M$.
$c \in N$: $m^{-1}n^{-1}m \in m^{-1}Nm = N$, so $c = (m^{-1}n^{-1}m)\,n$ is a product of two elements of $N$.
Hence $c \in M \cap N = (e)$, i.e. $m^{-1}n^{-1}mn = e$, which gives $mn = nm$. (This is a key step in recognising a group as an internal direct product $G \cong M \times N$.)

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.3 - If $(ab)^2 = a^2 b^2$ for all $a, b$, then $G$ is abelian
problems.problem: If $G$ is a group such that $(a \cdot b)^2 = a^2 \cdot b^2$ for all $a, b \in G$, show that $G$ must be abelian.
problems.hint: • Expand $(ab)^2 = abab$ and cancel.
problems.solution:
Let $a, b \in G$. The hypothesis says $abab = aabb$. Cancelling $a$ on the left (multiply by $a^{-1}$) gives $bab = abb$, and cancelling $b$ on the right gives $ba = ab$.
Since $a, b$ were arbitrary, $G$ is abelian. (Conversely, in an abelian group $(ab)^2 = a^2 b^2$ always holds, by Problem 2.)

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.4 - $(ab)^i = a^i b^i$ for three consecutive integers $i$ forces $G$ to be abelian
problems.problem: If $G$ is a group in which $(a \cdot b)^i = a^i \cdot b^i$ for three consecutive integers $i$ for all $a, b \in G$, show that $G$ is abelian.
problems.hint: • From the identities for $i$ and $i + 1$, deduce $b^i a = a b^i$. Similarly from $i + 1$ and $i + 2$, $b^{i+1} a = a b^{i+1}$. Then compare.
problems.solution:
Let the three consecutive integers be $i, i + 1, i + 2$, and fix $a, b \in G$.
Step 1. From $(ab)^{i+1} = (ab)^i (ab)$ we get $a^{i+1} b^{i+1} = a^i b^i a b$. Cancelling $a^i$ on the left and $b$ on the right: \[ a b^i = b^i a. \tag{1} \] In the same way, from $(ab)^{i+2} = (ab)^{i+1}(ab)$ we get $a^{i+2} b^{i+2} = a^{i+1} b^{i+1} a b$, hence \[ a b^{i+1} = b^{i+1} a. \tag{2} \]
Step 2. Using (1), \[ b^{i+1} a = b \,(b^i a) = b \,(a b^i) = (ba)\, b^i, \] while $a b^{i+1} = (ab)\, b^i$. By (2) these are equal: $(ba) b^i = (ab) b^i$. Cancelling $b^i$ on the right gives $ba = ab$.
So $G$ is abelian. (The argument works for negative $i$ as well, since the laws of exponents hold for all integers.)

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.5 - Two consecutive integers are not enough
problems.problem: Show that the conclusion of Problem 4 does not follow if we assume the relation $(a \cdot b)^i = a^i \cdot b^i$ for just two consecutive integers.
problems.hint: • Try $i = 0, 1$. For a less trivial example, use a nonabelian group in which $x^6 = e$ for every $x$.
problems.solution:
Trivial example. For $i = 0$ and $i = 1$ the relation reads $e = e$ and $ab = ab$, which hold in every group, including the nonabelian group $S_3$.
A less trivial example. Every element of $S_3$ has order $1$, $2$ or $3$, so $x^6 = e$ for all $x \in S_3$. Hence for all $a, b \in S_3$: \[ (ab)^6 = e = a^6 b^6, \qquad (ab)^7 = ab = a^7 b^7. \] So the relation holds for the two consecutive integers $6$ and $7$, but $S_3$ is not abelian.
What the two identities do give (Step 1 of Problem 4) is that every $i$-th power commutes with everything, i.e. $b^i$ lies in the center of $G$; in $S_3$ with $i = 6$ this says only that $e$ is central.

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.9 - Groups with three, four or five elements are abelian
problems.problem:
1. If the group $G$ has three elements, show it must be abelian.
  2. Do part (a) if $G$ has four elements.
  3. Do part (a) if $G$ has five elements.
problems.hint:
• If $ab \neq ba$, show that $e, a, b, ab, ba$ are five distinct elements.
  • For (c), the group would be exactly $\{ e, a, b, ab, ba \}$; ask where $a^2$ and $aba$ can be.
problems.solution:
Key lemma. If $ab \neq ba$, then $e, a, b, ab, ba$ are five distinct elements.
  • $a \neq e$, $b \neq e$ and $a \neq b$, since $e$ commutes with everything and $a$ commutes with itself.
  • $ab \notin \{ e, a, b \}$: $ab = e$ means $b = a^{-1}$, which commutes with $a$; $ab = a$ means $b = e$; $ab = b$ means $a = e$. Likewise $ba \notin \{ e, a, b \}$.
  • $ab \neq ba$ by assumption.
(a) and (b). A nonabelian group has at least $5$ elements by the lemma. So every group with $3$ or $4$ (indeed at most $4$) elements is abelian.
(c) Suppose $|G| = 5$ and $ab \neq ba$. By the lemma, $G = \{ e, a, b, ab, ba \}$.
  • Where is $a^2$? $a^2 \neq a$ (else $a = e$), $a^2 \neq ab$ and $a^2 \neq ba$ (else $a = b$), and $a^2 \neq b$ (else $b$ would commute with $a$). So $a^2 = e$, i.e. $a^{-1} = a$.
  • Where is $aba$? $aba = e$ gives $ab = a^{-1} = a$, so $b = e$. $aba = a$ gives $ba = e$, so $b = a^{-1} = a$. $aba = b$ gives $ab = ba^{-1} = ba$. $aba = ab$ gives $a = e$. $aba = ba$ gives $ab = b$, so $a = e$.
Every case is impossible, so no such $a, b$ exist: a group with five elements is abelian.
(With Lagrange's theorem of the next section there is a quicker proof: a group of prime order is cyclic. The lemma shows more: the smallest nonabelian group has order $6$, and $S_3$ is an example.)

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.10 - If every element is its own inverse, $G$ is abelian
problems.problem: Show that if every element of the group $G$ has its own inverse, then $G$ is abelian.
problems.hint: • Apply the hypothesis to $a$, $b$ and $ab$, and use $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1} a^{-1}$.
problems.solution:
Let $a, b \in G$. By hypothesis $a^{-1} = a$, $b^{-1} = b$ and $(ab)^{-1} = ab$. Hence \[ ab = (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1} a^{-1} = ba. \] So $G$ is abelian.
Equivalently: if $x^2 = e$ for all $x \in G$, then $G$ is abelian. Examples are $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ and, more generally, the subsets of a set under symmetric difference.

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.11 - A group of even order has an element $a \neq e$ with $a^2 = e$
problems.problem: If $G$ is a group of even order, prove it has an element $a \neq e$ satisfying $a^2 = e$.
problems.hint: • Pair each element $x$ with $x^{-1}$. The elements with $x \neq x^{-1}$ come in pairs.
problems.solution:
Note that $x^2 = e \iff x = x^{-1}$. Partition $G$ into the sets $\{ x, x^{-1} \}$. Each such set has two elements if $x \neq x^{-1}$, and one element if $x = x^{-1}$.
So the elements with $x \neq x^{-1}$ can be grouped into disjoint pairs, and their number is even. Hence the number of elements with $x = x^{-1}$, which is $|G|$ minus this even number, is even too.
The identity $e$ is one element with $e = e^{-1}$. Since their number is even, there is at least one more: some $a \neq e$ with $a = a^{-1}$, i.e. $a^2 = e$.
(The argument shows that the number of elements of order $2$ in a group of even order is odd.)

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.12 - A right identity and right inverses are enough for a group
problems.problem:
Let $G$ be a nonempty set closed under an associative product, which in addition satisfies:
  1. There exists an $e \in G$ such that $a \cdot e = a$ for all $a \in G$.
  2. Given $a \in G$, there exists an element $y(a) \in G$ such that $a \cdot y(a) = e$.
Prove that $G$ must be a group under this product.
problems.hint: • Show first that if $u \cdot u = u$, then $u = e$. Then apply this to $u = y(a) \cdot a$.
problems.solution:
Idempotents are trivial. If $u \cdot u = u$, then \[ u = u e = u\, (u\, y(u)) = (u u)\, y(u) = u\, y(u) = e. \]
Right inverses are left inverses. Let $a \in G$ and $y = y(a)$. Then \[ (y a)(y a) = y\, (a y)\, a = y\, e\, a = (y e)\, a = y a. \] So $ya$ is idempotent, and therefore $y a = e$. Thus $y(a)$ is a two-sided inverse of $a$.
$e$ is a left identity. $e a = (a\, y(a))\, a = a\, (y(a)\, a) = a e = a$. So $e$ is a two-sided identity.
Hence $G$ is associative, has a two-sided identity $e$, and every element has a two-sided inverse: $G$ is a group.

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.13 - A right identity with left inverses need not give a group
problems.problem:
Prove, by an example, that the conclusion of Problem 12 is false if we assume instead:
  1. There exists an $e \in G$ such that $a \cdot e = a$ for all $a \in G$.
  2. Given $a \in G$, there exists $y(a) \in G$ such that $y(a) \cdot a = e$.
problems.hint: • Try the product $a \cdot b = a$ on a set with at least two elements.
problems.solution:
Let $G$ be any set with at least two elements, and define $a \cdot b = a$ for all $a, b \in G$.
Associative: $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot c = a$ and $a \cdot (b \cdot c) = a \cdot b = a$.
Condition (a): fix any $e \in G$. Then $a \cdot e = a$ for all $a$.
Condition (b): take $y(a) = e$ for every $a$. Then $y(a) \cdot a = e \cdot a = e$.
Not a group. In a group, $x \cdot a = x \cdot b$ implies $a = b$. Here $x \cdot a = x = x \cdot b$ for all $a \neq b$, so left cancellation fails. (Equivalently, $e \cdot a = e \neq a$ for $a \neq e$, so $e$ is not a two-sided identity.) So mixing a right identity with left inverses is not enough.

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.14 - A finite set with an associative product and both cancellation laws is a group
problems.problem: Suppose a finite set $G$ is closed under an associative product and that both cancellation laws hold in $G$. Prove that $G$ must be a group.
problems.hint: • For fixed $a$, the maps $x \mapsto xa$ and $x \mapsto ax$ are one-to-one, hence onto (finiteness). Find a right identity and right inverses, then use Problem 12.
problems.solution:
(We assume $G \neq \varnothing$.) For $a \in G$, the maps $R_a(x) = xa$ and $L_a(x) = ax$ of $G$ into itself are one-to-one, by right and left cancellation. Since $G$ is finite, they are also onto.
A right identity. Fix $a_0 \in G$. Since $L_{a_0}$ is onto, there is $e$ with $a_0 e = a_0$. Let $b \in G$ be arbitrary. Since $R_{a_0}$ is onto, $b = x a_0$ for some $x$, and then \[ b e = x a_0 e = x a_0 = b. \] So $b e = b$ for all $b \in G$.
Right inverses. For $a \in G$, since $L_a$ is onto, there is $y$ with $a y = e$.
By Problem 12, $G$ is a group.
Finiteness is essential: see Problem 17.

problems.title: Herstein (Topics in Algebra) - 2.3.15 - The nonzero residues mod $p$, and the units mod $n$, are groups
problems.problem:
