The elements of $S_3$ are $(1), (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3), (1\ 2\ 3)$ and $(1\ 3\ 2)$. Note that \begin{align*} (1)^2 & = (1) \\ (1\ 2)^2 & = (1) \\ (1\ 3)^2 & = (1) \\ (2\ 3)^2 & = (1) \\ (1\ 2\ 3)^2 & = (1\ 3\ 2) \neq (1) \\ (1\ 3\ 2)^2 & = (1\ 2\ 3) \neq (1). \end{align*} Thus, there are four elements $x$ such that $x^2 = (1)$, which are $(1), (1\ 2), (1\ 3)$ and $(2\ 3)$.
Also, \begin{align*} (1)^3 & = (1) \\ (1\ 2)^3 & = (1\ 2) \neq (1) \\ (1\ 3)^3 & = (1\ 3) \neq (1) \\ (2\ 3)^3 & = (2\ 3) \neq (1) \\ (1\ 2\ 3)^3 & = (1) \\ (1\ 3\ 2)^3 & = (1). \end{align*} Thus, there are three elements $y$ such that $y^3 = (1)$, which are $(1), (1\ 2\ 3)$ and $(1\ 3\ 2)$.
Note that the elements $(1\ 2), (1\ 3)$ and $(2\ 3)$ are called transpositions and they are of order $2$. Geometrically, they can be thought of as reflections of an equilateral triangle. The element $(1)$ is the identity element and it is of order $1$. The elements $(1\ 2\ 3)$ and $(1\ 3\ 2)$ are called $3$-cycles and they are of order $3$. Geometrically, they can be thought of as rotations of an equilateral triangle.

problems.title: Herstein - If $G$ is a finite group, show that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that $a^N = e$ for all $a \in G$.
problems.problem: If $G$ is a finite group, show that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that $a^N = e$ for all $a \in G$.
problems.hint: • Note that if $a$ is an element of order $m$, then $a^m = e$. So, if we take $N$ to be a common multiple of the orders of all the elements in $G$, then we will have $a^N = e$ for all $a \in G$.
problems.solution: Let $G = \{ g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k \} $ be a finite group. For each $g_i \in G$, let $o(g_i) = n_i$ denote the order of $g_i$. Let \[ N = \mathrm{lcm} (n_1, n_2, \dots, n_k). \] Let $a \in G$ with $o(a) = m$. Since $N$ is a multiple of each $n_i$, we have \[ a^N = a^{m \cdot \frac{N}{m}} = (a^m)^{\frac{N}{m}} = e^{\frac{N}{m}} = e. \]

problems.title: NBHM 2005 - Units in Z[sqrt{3}]
problems.problem:
Pick out the units in $\mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{3} ]$
  1. $-7 + 4 \sqrt{3} $
  2. $5 + 3 \sqrt{3} $
  3. $2 - \sqrt{3} $
  4. $-3 - 2\sqrt{3} $.
problems.hint: • Check if there exists $c + d \sqrt{3} \in \mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{3} ]$ such that $(a + b \sqrt{3})(c + d \sqrt{3}) = 1$ for each of the given elements.
problems.solution:
Recall that an element $a + b \sqrt{3} \in \mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{3} ]$ is a unit if there exists $c + d \sqrt{3} \in \mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{3} ]$ such that \[ (a + b \sqrt{3})(c + d \sqrt{3}) = 1. \]
  1. Note that \begin{align*} & (-7 + 4 \sqrt{3})(a + b \sqrt{3}) = 1 \\ \implies & -7a + 4 \cdot 3 b + (-7b + 4a) \sqrt{3} = 1 \\ \implies & -7a + 12 b = 1 \text{ and } -7b + 4a = 0 \\ \implies & a = -7 \text{ and } b = -4. \end{align*} Thus, $-7 + 4 \sqrt{3} $ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{3} ]$.
  2. For $5 + 3 \sqrt{3} $, we have \begin{align*} & (5 + 3 \sqrt{3})(a + b \sqrt{3}) = 1 \\ \implies & 5a + 9b + (5b + 3a) \sqrt{3} = 1 \\ \implies & 5a + 9b = 1 \text{ and } 5b + 3a = 0 \\ \implies & a = -\frac{5}{2} \text{ and } b = \frac{3}{2}, \end{align*} which are not integers. Thus, $5 + 3 \sqrt{3} $ is not a unit in $\mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{3} ]$.
  3. For $2 - \sqrt{3} $, note that \begin{align*} & (2 - \sqrt{3})(a + b \sqrt{3}) = 1 \\ \implies & 2a - 3b + (2b - a) \sqrt{3} = 1 \\ \implies & 2a - 3b = 1 \text{ and } 2b - a = 0 \\ \implies & a = 2 \text{ and } b = 1. \end{align*} Thus, $2 - \sqrt{3} $ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{3} ]$.
  4. For $-3 - 2\sqrt{3} $, we have \begin{align*} & (-3 - 2\sqrt{3})(a + b \sqrt{3}) = 1 \\ \implies & -3a - 6b + (-3b - 2a) \sqrt{3} = 1 \\ \implies & -3a - 6b = 1 \text{ and } -3b - 2a = 0 \\ \implies & a = 1 \text{ and } b = -\frac{2}{3}, \end{align*} which are not integers. Thus, $-3 - 2\sqrt{3} $ is not a unit in $\mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{3} ]$.
In the ring $(\mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{d} ], \cdot)$, where $d$ is a square free number, $d \neq 0, d\neq 1$, the number $a + \sqrt{d} \in \mathbb{Z} [\sqrt{d} ]$ is a unit if and only if $a^2 - db^2 = \pm 1. $

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.1 - Intersection of two subgroups
problems.problem: If $A, B$ are subgroups of $G$, show that $A \cap B$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • We need to show that for any $x, y \in A \cap B$, $x \cdot y^{-1} \in A \cap B$.
problems.solution:
Let $A$ and $B$ be subgroups of $G$. We will show that $A \cap B$ is a subgroup of $G$. Note that $e \in A$ and $e \in B$, so $e \in A \cap B$, which implies that $A \cap B$ is non-empty.
Let $x,y \in A \cap B$. Since $A$ is a subgroup, we have $x^{-1} \in A$ and since $B$ is a subgroup, we have $x^{-1} \in B$. Thus, $x^{-1} \in A \cap B$.
Also, since $A$ is a subgroup, we have $x\cdot y \in A$ and since $B$ is a subgroup, we have $x\cdot y \in B$. Thus, $x\cdot y \in A \cap B$. Therefore, by the subgroup test, we conclude that $A \cap B$ is a subgroup of $G$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.2 - Cyclic subgroup of Z generated by -1
problems.problem: What is the cyclic subgroup of $\mathbb{Z} $ generated by $-1$ under $+$?
problems.hint: • Note that $-n = n\cdot (-1)$ and being a subgroup, the inverse will also be there.
problems.solution: We need to find the cyclic subgroup of $\mathbb{Z} $ generated by $-1$ under $+$. Note that for any $n \in \mathbb{Z} $ we have \begin{align*} -n & = \underbrace{(-1) + (-1) + \dots + (-1)}_{n \text{ times}} \\ & = n \cdot (-1). \end{align*} Thus, $-n \in \left\langle -1 \right\rangle $ which is a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z} $ which implies $n \in \left\langle -1 \right\rangle $ and hence $\mathbb{Z} \subseteq \left\langle -1 \right\rangle $. Therefore, $\left\langle -1 \right\rangle = \mathbb{Z} $.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.3 - Subgroups of S_3
problems.problem: Let $S_3$ be the symmetric group of degree $3.$  Find all subgroups of $S_3$.
problems.hint: • Note that if $G$ is a group and $H$ a nonempty finite subset of $G$ which is closed under the product in $G$. Then $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.solution:
The elements of $S_3$ are $(1), (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3), (1\ 2\ 3)$ and $(1\ 3\ 2)$. Note that the order of $S_3$ is $6$. We will use Lemma 2.3.2 from the Herstein book which states that if \textcolor{blue}{$G$ is a group and $H$ a nonempty finite subset of $G$ which is closed under the product in $G$. Then $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.}
Note that $(1\ 2)^2 = (1 \ 3)^2 = (2 \ 3)^2 = (1)$ and $(1 \ 2\ 3)^2 = (1 \ 3\ 2)$. Thus, the subgroups of $S_3$ are as follows:
  • $\{ (1) \}$, which is the trivial subgroup.
  • $\{ (1), (1\ 2) \}$, which is a subgroup of order $2$.
  • $\{ (1), (1\ 3) \}$, which is a subgroup of order $2$.
  • $\{ (1), (2\ 3) \}$, which is a subgroup of order $2$.
  • $\{ (1), (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3\ 2) \}$, which is a subgroup of order $3$.
  • $S_3$ itself, which is a subgroup of order $6$.
For other possibilities, note that if we take any two distinct transpositions, say $(1\ 2)$ and $(1\ 3)$, then we will have $(1\ 2)(1\ 3) = (1\ 2\ 3)$ and $(1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 3\ 2)$, which are not in the subgroup generated by $(1\ 2)$ and $(1\ 3)$. Thus, there is no subgroup of order $4$. Also, if we take any transposition, say $(1\ 2)$ and any $3$-cycle, say $(1\ 2\ 3)$, then we will have $(1\ 2)(1\ 2\ 3) = (1\ 3)$ and $(1\ 2\ 3)(1\ 2) = (2\ 3)$, which are not in the subgroup generated by $(1\ 2)$ and $(1\ 2\ 3)$. Thus, there is no subgroup of order $6$ other than $S_3$ itself.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.4 - Center of a group is subgroup
problems.problem: Verify that $Z(G)$, the center of $G$, is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • Use the subgroup test to show that $Z(G)$ is a subgroup of $G$. That is, show that for any $x,y \in Z(G)$, $x \cdot y^{-1} \in Z(G)$.
problems.solution: We will show that $Z(G)$ is a subgroup of $G$. At first recall that \[ Z(G) = \{ z \in G : zg = gz \text{ for all } g \in G \}. \] Note that $e \in Z(G)$, so $Z(G) \neq \varnothing $. Let $x,y \in Z(G)$. We will show that $x\cdot y^{-1} \in Z(G)$. Let $g \in G$ be arbitrary. Since $x,y \in Z(G)$, we have \begin{align*} g \cdot (x \cdot y^{-1}) & = (g \cdot x) \cdot y^{-1} = (x \cdot g) \cdot y^{-1} = x \cdot (g \cdot y^{-1}) \\ & = x \cdot (y^{-1} \cdot g) = (x \cdot y^{-1}) \cdot g. \end{align*} Thus, $x \cdot y^{-1} \in Z(G)$. Therefore, by the subgroup test, we conclude that $Z(G)$ is a subgroup of $G$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.5 - Center of a group is intersection of centralizers
problems.problem:
If $C(a)$ is the centralizer of $a$ in $G$, prove that 
    \[
        Z(G) = \bigcap_{a \in G} C(a).
    \]
problems.hint: • Note that $C(a) = \{ g \in G : ga = ag \}.$
problems.solution:
Recall that the centralizer of $a$ in $G$ is defined as \[ C(a) = \{ g \in G : ga = ag \}. \] We will show that $Z(G) = \bigcap_{a \in G} C(a)$.
First, let $z \in Z(G)$. Then, for any $a \in G$, we have $za = az$. This means $z \in C(a)$ for all $a \in G$. Therefore, $z \in \bigcap_{a \in G} C(a)$.
Conversely, let $z \in \bigcap_{a \in G} C(a)$. Then, for any $a \in G$, we have $z \in C(a)$, which means $za = az$. Since this holds for all $a \in G$, we conclude that $z \in Z(G)$.
Thus, $Z(G) = \bigcap_{a \in G} C(a)$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.6 - Center of a group is the set of elements whose centralizer is the whole group
problems.problem: Show that $a \in Z(G)$ if and only if $C(a) = G$.
problems.hint: • Note that $C(a) = \{ g \in G : ga = ag \}.$
problems.solution:
We need to show that $a \in Z(G)$ if and only if $C(a) = G$. Recall that $Z(G) = \{ z \in G : zg = gz \text{ for all } g \in G \}$ and $C(a) = \{ g \in G : ga = ag \}.$
First, let $a \in Z(G)$. Then, for any $g \in G$, we have $ag = ga$. This means $g \in C(a)$ for all $g \in G$. Therefore, $C(a) = G$.
Conversely, let $C(a) = G$. Then, for any $g \in G$, we have $g \in C(a)$, which means $ga = ag$. Since this holds for all $g \in G$, we conclude that $a \in Z(G)$.
Thus, $a \in Z(G)$ if and only if $C(a) = G$.

problems.title: Number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order 8
problems.problem: Find the number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $8$.
problems.hint: • Use the fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups.
problems.solution:
The order of the group is $8 = 2^3$. The number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $p^n$ (where $p$ is a prime and $n$ is a positive integer) is equal to the number of partitions of $n$. The partitions of $3$ are as follows:
  • $3$
  • $2 + 1$
  • $1 + 1 + 1$
Thus, there are three non-isomorphic abelian groups of order $8$, which are $\mathbb{Z} _8$, $\mathbb{Z} _4 \times \mathbb{Z} _2$ and $\mathbb{Z} _2 \times \mathbb{Z} _2 \times \mathbb{Z} _2$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.7 - Centralizer of elements in S_3
problems.problem: In $S_3$, find $C(a)$ for each $a \in S_3$.
problems.hint: • Note that $C(a) = \{ g \in S_3 : ga = ag \}.$ Look at geometrically what the elements of $S_3$ represent and try to find the elements that commute with each element of $S_3$.
problems.solution:
The elements of $S_3$ are $(1), (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3), (1\ 2\ 3)$ and $(1\ 3\ 2)$. We will find $C(a)$ for each $a \in S_3$.
For $a = (1)$, we have $C((1)) = S_3$ since the identity element commutes with all elements of the group.
For $a = (1\ 2)$, we have \begin{align*} C((1\ 2)) & = \{ g \in S_3 : g(1\ 2) = (1\ 2)g \} \\ & = \{ (1), (1\ 2) \}. \end{align*}
For $a = (1\ 3)$, we have \begin{align*} C((1\ 3)) & = \{ g \in S_3 : g(1\ 3) = (1\ 3)g \} \\ & = \{ (1), (1\ 3) \}. \end{align*}
For $a = (2\ 3)$, we have \begin{align*} C((2\ 3)) & = \{ g \in S_3 : g(2\ 3) = (2\ 3)g \} \\ & = \{ (1), (2\ 3) \}. \end{align*}
For $a = (1\ 2\ 3)$, we have \begin{align*} C((1\ 2\ 3)) & = \{ g \in S_3 : g(1\ 2\ 3) = (1\ 2\ 3)g \} \\ & = \{ (1), (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3\ 2) \}. \end{align*}'=
For $a = (1\ 3\ 2)$, we have \begin{align*} C((1\ 3\ 2)) & = \{ g \in S_3 : g(1\ 3\ 2) = (1\ 3\ 2)g \} \\ & = \{ (1), (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3\ 2) \}. \end{align*}

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.8 - Subgroup of elements of order 2 in an abelian group
problems.problem: If $G$ is an abelian group and $H = \{ a \in G \mid a^2 = e \} $, show that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • Note that for an abelian group $(ab)^2 = a^2 b^2$.
problems.solution: Let $G$ be an abelian group and $H = \{ a \in G \mid a^2 = e \} $. We will show that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$. Note that $e ^2 = e \implies e \in H$, so $H$ is non-empty. Let $x,y \in H$. Then, we have \[ x^2 = e \text{ and } y^2 = e. \] We will show that $x\cdot y^{-1} \in H$. Since $G$ is abelian, we have \begin{align*} (x\cdot y^{-1})^2 & = x\cdot y^{-1} \cdot x\cdot y^{-1} \\ & = x\cdot x\cdot y^{-1}\cdot y^{-1} \\ & = x^2\cdot (y^{-1})^2 = e\cdot e = e. \end{align*} Thus, $x\cdot y^{-1} \in H$. Therefore, by the subgroup test, we conclude that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.9 - Is the set of elements of order 2 a subgroup in a non-abelian group?
problems.problem: Previously we showed that if $G$ is an abelian group and $H = \{ a \in G \mid a^2 = e \} $, then $H$ is a subgroup of $G$. Is the same true if $G$ is not abelian?
problems.hint: • Consider the symmetric group $S_3$ and the set $H = \{ a \in S_3 \mid a^2 = e \} $. Check if $H$ is closed under the product in $S_3$.
problems.solution: The answer is no. Let $G = S_3$ and $H = \{ a \in G \mid a^2 = e \} $. Then, we have \[ H = \{ (1), (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3) \}. \] Note that $(1\ 2)(1\ 3) = (1\ 2\ 3) \notin H$. Thus, $H$ is not closed under the product in $G$. Therefore, $H$ is not a subgroup of $G$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.10 - Subgroup of elements of the form a^n in an abelian group
problems.problem: If $G$ is an abelian group and $n > 1$ an integer, let $A_n = \{ a^n: a \in G \} $. Prove that $A_n$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • Note that for an abelian group $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
problems.solution:
Given that $G$ is an abelian group and \[ A_n = \{ a^n : a \in G \}, \quad n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ and } n > 1. \] We want to prove that $A_n$ is a subgroup of $G$.
Note that $e^n = e$, so $e \in A_n$. Let $a^n \text{ and } b^n \in A_n$. Them, we have \begin{align*} \left( a^n \right) \cdot \left( b^n \right) ^{-1} & = a^n \cdot (b^{-1})^n \\ & = a^n \cdot (b^{-1})^n \\ & = (a \cdot b^{-1})^n \in A_n, \end{align*} where the last step is valid because $G$ is abelian. Thus, by the subgroup test, we conclude that $A_n$ is a subgroup of $G$.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.11 - Subgroup of elements of finite order in an abelian group
problems.problem:
If $G$ is an abelian group and 
    \[
        H = \left\{ a \in G: a^{n(a)} = e, \text{ for some } n(a) > 1 \text{ depending on } a \right\}, 
    \] 
    prove that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • Note that for an abelian group $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
problems.solution: Note that $e \in H$ since $e^{n(e)} = e$ for any $n(e) = 1$. Let $x,y \in H$. Then, we have \[ x^{n(x)} = e \text{ and } y^{n(y)} = e. \] As $G$ is abelian, for any $n \in \mathbb{Z} $ we have $(x\cdot y)^n = x^n \cdot y^n$. Now consider \begin{align*} (x \cdot y^{-1})^{n(x) n(y)} & = x^{n(x) n(y)} \cdot (y^{-1})^{n(x) n(y)} \\ & = (x^{n(x)})^{n(y)} \cdot ((y^{-1})^{n(y)})^{n(x)} \\ & = e^{n(y)} \cdot e^{n(x)} = e. \end{align*}

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.12 - Cyclic group is abelian
problems.problem: Prove that a cyclic group is abelian.
problems.hint: • In a group $g^m \cdot g^n = g^{m + n} $.
problems.solution: Let $G$ be a cyclic group generated by $g$. We claim that $G$ is cyclic. Let $a,b \in G$. Then, we have $a = g^m$ and $b = g^n$ for some integers $m,n$. Thus, \begin{align*} a \cdot b & = g^m \cdot g^n = g^{m+n} = g^{n+m} \\ & = g^n \cdot g^m = b \cdot a. \end{align*} Therefore, $G$ is abelian.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.13 - Subgroup of cyclic group is cyclic
problems.problem: If $G$ is cyclic, show that every subgroup of $G$ is cyclic.
problems.hint: • Show that if $G = \left\langle g \right\rangle $, then for any subgroup $H$ of $G$, there exists an integer $n > 0$ ($n = \min \{ k \in \mathbb{N} : g^k \in H \} $ ) such that $g^n \in H$. Then, show that $H = \left\langle g^n \right\rangle $.
problems.solution: Let $G$ be a cyclic group generated by $g$. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. If $H = \{ e \}$, then $H$ is cyclic. Now, let $H \neq \{ e \}$. Then, there exists an integer $m > 0$ such that $g^m \in H$. By the well-ordering principle, let \[ n = \min \{ k \in \mathbb{N} : g^k \in H \}. \] We claim that $H = \langle g^n \rangle $. Let $h \in H$. Then, we have $h = g^k$ for some integer $k$. By the division algorithm, we can write \[ k = nq + r, \] where $q,r$ are integers and $0 \leq r < n$. Thus, we have \[ h = g^k = g^{nq + r} = (g^n)^q g^r. \] Since $(g^n)^q \in H$, we have $g^r = h (g^n)^{-q} \in H$. By the minimality of $n$, we must have $r = 0$. Thus, we have \[ h = (g^n)^q. \] Therefore, we conclude that every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.14 - Group with no proper subgroups is cyclic
problems.problem: If $G$ has no proper subgroups, prove that $G$ is cyclic.
problems.hint: • Note that for any $a \in G$, $\langle a \rangle$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.solution: Let $G$ be a group with no proper subgroups. If $G = \{ e \}$, then $G$ is cyclic. Now, let $G \neq \{ e \}$. Let $a \in G$ with $a \neq e$. Then, we have $\langle a \rangle$ is a subgroup of $G$. Since $G$ has no proper subgroups, we must have $\langle a \rangle = G$. Thus, we conclude that $G$ is cyclic.

problems.title: Herstein - 2.3.15 - If a nonempty subset is closed under ab^{-1}, then it is a subgroup
problems.problem: If $G$ is a group and $H$ a nonempty subset of $G$ such that, given $a,b \in H$, then $a b^{-1} \in H$, prove that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.
problems.hint: • Note that $e \in H$ (as $H$ is nonempty) and $H$ is closed under inversion.
problems.solution:
We are given that $H$ is a nonempty subset of $G$ such that for any $a,b \in H$, we have $ab^{-1} \in H$. We will show that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$. Note that since $H$ is nonempty, there exists an element $h \in H$. Since $h \in H$, we have $hh^{-1} = e \in H$.
Note that for any $h \in H$, we have $e h^{-1} = h^{-1} \in H$. Thus, $H$ is closed under taking inverses.
Now we will show that $H$ is closed under the group operation. Let $x, y \in H$. Then, we have $y^{-1} \in H$. Thus, we have $x (y^{-1})^{-1} \in H$ which implies $xy \in H$. Therefore, by the subgroup test, we conclude that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.

problems.title: A nonempty finite subset closed under the product is a subgroup
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a group and let $H$ be a nonempty finite subset of $G$ such that $ab \in H$ whenever $a, b \in H$. Prove that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$. Show by an example that finiteness cannot be dropped.
problems.hint: • For $a \in H$, all powers $a, a^2, a^3, \dots$ lie in the finite set $H$, so two of them coincide.
problems.solution:
Since $H$ is closed under the product, it only remains to show that $e \in H$ and that $H$ contains the inverse of each of its elements.
Let $a \in H$. Then $a, a^2, a^3, \dots$ all lie in $H$. As $H$ is finite, these cannot all be distinct: $a^m = a^n$ for some $m \gt n \geq 1$. Multiplying by $a^{-n}$ in $G$ gives $a^{m - n} = e$, where $k \coloneqq m - n \geq 1$. Hence $e = a^k \in H$.
If $k = 1$, then $a = e$ and $a^{-1} = e \in H$. If $k \geq 2$, then $a \cdot a^{k-1} = a^k = e$, so $a^{-1} = a^{k-1} \in H$. Thus $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.
Finiteness is needed. In the group $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$, the subset $\mathbb{N} = \{ 1, 2, 3, \dots \}$ is nonempty and closed under addition, but it is not a subgroup (it does not contain $0$, nor $-1$).

problems.title: If $a^2 = e$ for every element $a$, the group is abelian
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a group in which $a^2 = e$ for every $a \in G$. Prove that $G$ is abelian.
problems.hint: • $a^2 = e$ means $a = a^{-1}$. Apply this to $a$, $b$ and $ab$.
problems.solution:
The hypothesis $a^2 = e$ says $a^{-1} = a$ for every $a \in G$.
Let $a, b \in G$. Applying this to $ab$, $a$ and $b$, \[ ab = (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1} a^{-1} = b a. \] Hence $G$ is abelian.

problems.title: If $(ab)^2 = a^2 b^2$ for all $a, b$, the group is abelian
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a group such that $(ab)^2 = a^2 b^2$ for all $a, b \in G$. Prove that $G$ is abelian.
problems.hint: • Expand $(ab)^2 = abab$ and cancel.
problems.solution:
Let $a, b \in G$. The hypothesis says \[ a b a b = a a b b. \] Multiplying on the left by $a^{-1}$ gives $b a b = a b b$, and multiplying on the right by $b^{-1}$ gives $b a = a b$. Since $a$ and $b$ were arbitrary, $G$ is abelian.
Remark. Conversely, in an abelian group $(ab)^2 = abab = aabb = a^2 b^2$. So this identity characterises abelian groups. The example $x = (1\,2)$, $y = (1\,3)$ in $S_3$ (see the problem of 11 March 2026) shows that it fails in non-abelian groups.

problems.title: The elements $ab$ and $ba$ have the same order
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a group and $a, b \in G$. Prove that $ab$ and $ba$ have the same order.
problems.hint:
• Show that $ba = a^{-1} (ab) a$, i.e. $ba$ is a conjugate of $ab$.
  • Conjugation $x \mapsto g^{-1} x g$ preserves powers: $(g^{-1} x g)^n = g^{-1} x^n g$.
problems.solution:
Observe that \[ a^{-1} (ab) a = (a^{-1} a)(b a) = ba. \] So $ba = g^{-1} x g$ with $x = ab$ and $g = a$.
For every $n \geq 1$, \[ (g^{-1} x g)^n = (g^{-1} x g)(g^{-1} x g) \cdots (g^{-1} x g) = g^{-1} x^n g, \] because the inner factors $g g^{-1}$ cancel. Hence \[ (ba)^n = e \iff a^{-1} (ab)^n a = e \iff (ab)^n = a a^{-1} = e. \]
So $(ab)^n = e$ and $(ba)^n = e$ hold for exactly the same positive integers $n$. If one of $ab$, $ba$ has finite order, the smallest such $n$ is the same for both; and if one has infinite order (no such $n$ exists), so does the other. Therefore $o(ab) = o(ba)$.

problems.title: In a cyclic group of order $n$, the order of $a^k$ is $n / \gcd(n, k)$
problems.problem: Let $G = \langle a \rangle$ be a cyclic group of order $n$ and let $k$ be an integer. Prove that the order of $a^k$ is $\frac{n}{\gcd(n, k)}$. Deduce that $a^k$ generates $G$ if and only if $\gcd(n, k) = 1$.
problems.hint:
• $a^m = e$ if and only if $n \mid m$. So $(a^k)^m = e$ if and only if $n \mid km$.
  • With $d = \gcd(n,k)$, write $n = d n'$ and $k = d k'$ with $\gcd(n', k') = 1$.
problems.solution:
Since $a$ has order $n$, for an integer $m$ we have $a^m = e$ if and only if $n \mid m$. Hence \[ (a^k)^m = e \iff a^{km} = e \iff n \mid km. \]
Let $d = \gcd(n, k)$ and write $n = d n'$, $k = d k'$, where $\gcd(n', k') = 1$. Then \[ n \mid km \iff d n' \mid d k' m \iff n' \mid k' m \iff n' \mid m, \] where the last step uses $\gcd(n', k') = 1$. So the smallest positive $m$ with $(a^k)^m = e$ is $m = n' = \frac{n}{d}$. That is, $o(a^k) = \frac{n}{\gcd(n, k)}$.
In particular, $a^k$ generates $G$ if and only if $o(a^k) = n$, i.e. if and only if $\gcd(n, k) = 1$. So a cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly $\varphi(n)$ generators. For example, in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ the element $8$ has order $\frac{12}{\gcd(12, 8)} = 3$, and the generators are $1, 5, 7, 11$.

problems.title: Find all subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$
problems.problem: Find all subgroups of the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_{12} = \{ 0, 1, \dots, 11 \}$ under addition modulo $12$, and draw their inclusions.
problems.hint: • Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic. For each divisor $d$ of $12$ there is exactly one subgroup of order $d$.
problems.solution:
Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic (problem of 8 July 2026), so every subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ is $\langle k \rangle$ for some $k$. By the problem of 26 August 2026, $\langle k \rangle$ has order $\frac{12}{\gcd(12, k)}$, and in fact $\langle k \rangle = \langle \gcd(12, k) \rangle$ (each generates the other, since $\gcd(12,k)$ is an integer combination of $12$ and $k$). So the subgroups are $\langle d \rangle$ for the divisors $d$ of $12$: \[ \begin{aligned} \langle 1 \rangle &= \mathbb{Z}_{12} && \text{(order } 12\text{)}, \\ \langle 2 \rangle &= \{ 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 \} && \text{(order } 6\text{)}, \\ \langle 3 \rangle &= \{ 0, 3, 6, 9 \} && \text{(order } 4\text{)}, \\ \langle 4 \rangle &= \{ 0, 4, 8 \} && \text{(order } 3\text{)}, \\ \langle 6 \rangle &= \{ 0, 6 \} && \text{(order } 2\text{)}, \\ \langle 0 \rangle &= \{ 0 \} && \text{(order } 1\text{)}. \end{aligned} \]
Inclusions: $\langle d \rangle \subseteq \langle d' \rangle$ exactly when $d' \mid d$. So \[ \{0\} \subset \langle 6 \rangle \subset \langle 3 \rangle \subset \mathbb{Z}_{12}, \qquad \langle 6 \rangle \subset \langle 2 \rangle, \qquad \{0\} \subset \langle 4 \rangle \subset \langle 2 \rangle \subset \mathbb{Z}_{12}. \] In total $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ has $6$ subgroups, one for each of the $6$ divisors of $12$.

problems.title: A group of prime order is cyclic
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a group of order $p$, where $p$ is a prime. Prove that $G$ is cyclic, and that every element other than $e$ generates $G$.
problems.hint: • By Lagrange's theorem the order of a subgroup divides $\vert G \vert$.
problems.solution:
Let $a \in G$ with $a \neq e$ (such an element exists since $p \geq 2$). The cyclic subgroup $\langle a \rangle$ contains at least the two elements $e$ and $a$, so $\vert \langle a \rangle \vert \geq 2$.
By Lagrange's theorem, $\vert \langle a \rangle \vert$ divides $\vert G \vert = p$. The only divisors of the prime $p$ are $1$ and $p$, so $\vert \langle a \rangle \vert = p$, i.e. $\langle a \rangle = G$. Hence $G$ is cyclic and every non-identity element is a generator. In particular $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_p$, and every group of prime order is abelian.

problems.title: The Klein four-group is not cyclic, and $U(8)$ is a Klein four-group
problems.problem:
Let $U(8) = \{ 1, 3, 5, 7 \}$ be the group of units modulo $8$ under multiplication.
  1. Show that every element of $U(8)$ satisfies $x^2 = 1$, and conclude that $U(8)$ is not cyclic.
  2. Show that $U(8)$ is isomorphic to the Klein four-group $V_4 = \{ e, a, b, ab \}$, where $a^2 = b^2 = e$ and $ab = ba$.
problems.hint: • A cyclic group of order $4$ has an element of order $4$.
problems.solution:
(i) Modulo $8$: $1^2 = 1$, $3^2 = 9 \equiv 1$, $5^2 = 25 \equiv 1$, $7^2 = 49 \equiv 1$. So every element has order $1$ or $2$. A cyclic group of order $4$ has a generator, which has order $4$; since $U(8)$ has no element of order $4$, it is not cyclic.
(ii) Note $3 \cdot 5 = 15 \equiv 7 \pmod 8$. Define $\phi : V_4 \to U(8)$ by \[ \phi(e) = 1, \quad \phi(a) = 3, \quad \phi(b) = 5, \quad \phi(ab) = 7. \] This is a bijection. Both groups are abelian, every non-identity element squares to the identity, and the product of any two distinct non-identity elements is the third one (in $U(8)$: $3 \cdot 5 \equiv 7$, $3 \cdot 7 = 21 \equiv 5$, $5 \cdot 7 = 35 \equiv 3$). Hence the multiplication tables correspond under $\phi$, so $\phi$ is an isomorphism and $U(8) \cong V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$.

problems.title: A subgroup of index $2$ is normal
problems.problem: Let $H$ be a subgroup of a group $G$ with $[G : H] = 2$. Prove that $H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$. Deduce that $A_n$ is normal in $S_n$.
problems.hint: • If there are only two left cosets, they are $H$ and $G \setminus H$. The same holds for right cosets.
problems.solution:
Since $[G : H] = 2$, there are exactly two left cosets of $H$. One of them is $H = eH$; as the cosets partition $G$, the other must be $G \setminus H$. The same argument shows that the two right cosets are $H$ and $G \setminus H$.
Let $g \in G$. If $g \in H$, then $gH = H = Hg$. If $g \notin H$, then $gH \neq H$ (as $g \in gH$), so $gH = G \setminus H$; likewise $Hg = G \setminus H$. In both cases $gH = Hg$, which means $H$ is normal in $G$.
Example. For $n \geq 2$, the alternating group $A_n$ has $\frac{n!}{2}$ elements, so $[S_n : A_n] = 2$ and therefore $A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$.

problems.title: $HK$ is a subgroup if and only if $HK = KH$
problems.problem: Let $H$ and $K$ be subgroups of a group $G$ and let $HK = \{ hk : h \in H, k \in K \}$. Prove that $HK$ is a subgroup of $G$ if and only if $HK = KH$.
problems.hint: • A subgroup is equal to the set of inverses of its elements. What is the set of inverses of the elements of $HK$?
problems.solution:
First note that the set of inverses of the elements of $HK$ is $KH$: \[ (hk)^{-1} = k^{-1} h^{-1} \in KH, \qquad \text{and} \qquad kh = (h^{-1} k^{-1})^{-1} \text{ with } h^{-1} k^{-1} \in HK. \] Write this as $(HK)^{-1} = KH$.
($\Rightarrow$) If $HK$ is a subgroup, it contains the inverses of its elements and every element is the inverse of an element of it, so $HK = (HK)^{-1} = KH$.
($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $HK = KH$. Clearly $e = ee \in HK$. For closure under products, let $h_1 k_1, h_2 k_2 \in HK$. Since $k_1 h_2 \in KH = HK$, write $k_1 h_2 = h_3 k_3$. Then \[ (h_1 k_1)(h_2 k_2) = h_1 (h_3 k_3) k_2 = (h_1 h_3)(k_3 k_2) \in HK. \] For inverses, $(hk)^{-1} \in (HK)^{-1} = KH = HK$. So $HK$ is a subgroup.
In particular, if $G$ is abelian, or if one of $H, K$ is normal in $G$, then $HK = KH$ and $HK$ is a subgroup. In $S_3$, with $H = \{ e, (1\,2) \}$ and $K = \{ e, (1\,3) \}$, the set $HK$ has $4$ elements, which does not divide $6$, so $HK$ is not a subgroup; consistently, $HK \neq KH$.

problems.title: The kernel of a homomorphism is a normal subgroup
problems.problem:
Let $\phi : G \to G'$ be a group homomorphism and let $\ker \phi = \{ g \in G : \phi(g) = e' \}$, where $e'$ is the identity of $G'$.
  1. Prove that $\ker \phi$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
  2. Prove that $\phi$ is one-to-one if and only if $\ker \phi = \{ e \}$.
problems.hint: • Recall that $\phi(e) = e'$ and $\phi(g^{-1}) = \phi(g)^{-1}$ for a homomorphism.
problems.solution:
Recall that a homomorphism satisfies $\phi(e) = e'$ (from $\phi(e) = \phi(e e) = \phi(e) \phi(e)$) and $\phi(g^{-1}) = \phi(g)^{-1}$ (from $\phi(g) \phi(g^{-1}) = \phi(e) = e'$).
(i) $e \in \ker \phi$. If $a, b \in \ker \phi$, then \[ \phi(a b^{-1}) = \phi(a) \phi(b)^{-1} = e' e'^{-1} = e', \] so $a b^{-1} \in \ker \phi$, and $\ker \phi$ is a subgroup. It is normal: for $g \in G$ and $k \in \ker \phi$, \[ \phi(g k g^{-1}) = \phi(g) \phi(k) \phi(g)^{-1} = \phi(g) \phi(g)^{-1} = e', \] so $g k g^{-1} \in \ker \phi$.
(ii) If $\phi$ is one-to-one, then $\phi(g) = e' = \phi(e)$ forces $g = e$, so $\ker \phi = \{ e \}$. Conversely, suppose $\ker \phi = \{ e \}$ and $\phi(a) = \phi(b)$. Then \[ \phi(a b^{-1}) = \phi(a) \phi(b)^{-1} = e', \] so $a b^{-1} \in \ker \phi = \{ e \}$, i.e. $a = b$. Hence $\phi$ is one-to-one.

problems.title: If $G / Z(G)$ is cyclic, then $G$ is abelian
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a group with centre $Z(G) = \{ z \in G : zg = gz \text{ for all } g \in G \}$. Prove that if the quotient group $G / Z(G)$ is cyclic, then $G$ is abelian.
problems.hint: • If $G / Z(G) = \langle g Z(G) \rangle$, every element of $G$ can be written as $g^m z$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $z \in Z(G)$.
problems.solution:
Write $Z = Z(G)$, which is a normal subgroup of $G$, and suppose $G / Z = \langle gZ \rangle$ for some $g \in G$. Every coset is a power of $gZ$, so for every $x \in G$ there is $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $xZ = (gZ)^m = g^m Z$, i.e. $x = g^m z$ for some $z \in Z$.
Now let $x, y \in G$ and write $x = g^m z_1$ and $y = g^n z_2$ with $z_1, z_2 \in Z$. Since $z_1, z_2$ commute with everything and powers of $g$ commute with each other, \[ xy = g^m z_1 g^n z_2 = g^m g^n z_1 z_2 = g^{m + n} z_2 z_1 = g^n g^m z_2 z_1 = g^n z_2 g^m z_1 = yx. \] Hence $G$ is abelian (and then, in fact, $Z = G$ and $G / Z$ is trivial).
This is often used in the contrapositive form: for a non-abelian group, $G / Z(G)$ is never cyclic. For example, it can never have prime order.

problems.title: In a finite group of even order, the number of elements of order $2$ is odd
problems.problem: Let $G$ be a finite group of even order. Prove that the number of elements of order $2$ in $G$ is odd. In particular, $G$ contains an element of order $2$.
problems.hint: • Pair each element $g$ with its inverse $g^{-1}$. Which elements are paired with themselves?
problems.solution:
Partition $G$ into the sets $\{ g, g^{-1} \}$. Such a set has two elements if $g \neq g^{-1}$, and one element if $g = g^{-1}$, i.e. if $g^2 = e$.
Let $S = \{ g \in G : g = g^{-1} \}$. The elements outside $S$ come in pairs $\{ g, g^{-1} \}$ with $g \neq g^{-1}$, so $\vert G \setminus S \vert$ is even. As $\vert G \vert$ is even, $\vert S \vert = \vert G \vert - \vert G \setminus S \vert$ is even.
Now $S$ consists of $e$ together with the elements of order $2$. Hence the number of elements of order $2$ is $\vert S \vert - 1$, which is odd. In particular it is at least $1$, so $G$ has an element of order $2$. (For example, $S_3$ has $3$ elements of order $2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ has $3$.)

problems.title: Find all group homomorphisms from $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ to $\mathbb{Z}_{18}$
problems.problem: Find all group homomorphisms $\phi : \mathbb{Z}_{12} \to \mathbb{Z}_{18}$ (both groups under addition).
problems.hint:
• A homomorphism from a cyclic group is determined by the image $x = \phi(1)$ of a generator. Which $x$ are allowed?
  • You need $12 x \equiv 0 \pmod{18}$.
problems.solution:
Since $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ is generated by $1$, a homomorphism is determined by $x = \phi(1) \in \mathbb{Z}_{18}$: then $\phi(k) = kx \bmod 18$. This formula gives a well-defined map exactly when $k \equiv k' \pmod{12}$ implies $kx \equiv k'x \pmod{18}$, i.e. when \[ 12 x \equiv 0 \pmod{18}. \] (Equivalently, the order of $x$ must divide $12$.) When this holds, $\phi(k) = kx$ is clearly additive, so it is a homomorphism.
Now $18 \mid 12x \iff 3 \mid 2x \iff 3 \mid x$. So the possible values are \[ x \in \{ 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 \}, \] and there are exactly $6$ homomorphisms, $\phi_x(k) = kx \bmod 18$ for these $x$.
This agrees with the general fact that there are $\gcd(m, n)$ homomorphisms $\mathbb{Z}_m \to \mathbb{Z}_n$; here $\gcd(12, 18) = 6$. For instance, $\phi_3$ has image $\langle 3 \rangle$ of order $6$ and kernel $\{ 0, 6 \}$, consistent with $12 / 2 = 6$.

problems.title: Conjugacy classes and the class equation of $S_3$
problems.problem: Find the conjugacy classes of the symmetric group $S_3$ and verify the class equation $\vert G \vert = \vert Z(G) \vert + \sum [G : C(a)]$, the sum running over one representative $a$ of each conjugacy class with more than one element.
problems.hint: • In $S_n$, two permutations are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type: $\sigma (a_1\, a_2 \cdots a_k) \sigma^{-1} = (\sigma(a_1)\, \sigma(a_2) \cdots \sigma(a_k))$.
problems.solution:
For $\sigma \in S_3$ we have $\sigma (a\, b) \sigma^{-1} = (\sigma(a)\, \sigma(b))$ and $\sigma (a\, b\, c) \sigma^{-1} = (\sigma(a)\, \sigma(b)\, \sigma(c))$. So conjugation preserves cycle type, and any two cycles of the same length are conjugate (choose $\sigma$ sending one to the other). Hence the conjugacy classes are \[ \{ e \}, \qquad \{ (1\,2), (1\,3), (2\,3) \}, \qquad \{ (1\,2\,3), (1\,3\,2) \}. \]
The centre of $S_3$ is $\{ e \}$, since no transposition or $3$-cycle commutes with everything. The centraliser of $(1\,2)$ is $\{ e, (1\,2) \}$, of index $3$; the centraliser of $(1\,2\,3)$ is $A_3 = \{ e, (1\,2\,3), (1\,3\,2) \}$, of index $2$. These indices equal the class sizes, as they must. The class equation reads \[ 6 = 1 + 3 + 2. \]

problems.title: Every group of order $p^2$ is abelian
problems.problem: Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be a group of order $p^2$. Prove that $G$ is abelian.
problems.hint:
• First use the class equation to show that $Z(G) \neq \{ e \}$.
  • Then use the problem of 14 October 2026: if $G / Z(G)$ is cyclic, $G$ is abelian.
problems.solution:
Step 1: the centre is non-trivial. The class equation gives \[ p^2 = \vert G \vert = \vert Z(G) \vert + \sum [G : C(a)], \] where the sum is over representatives of the conjugacy classes with more than one element. For such $a$, $C(a)$ is a proper subgroup, so $[G : C(a)]$ is a divisor of $p^2$ greater than $1$, hence divisible by $p$. Therefore $p$ divides $\vert Z(G) \vert$. Since $e \in Z(G)$, $\vert Z(G) \vert \geq 1$, hence $\vert Z(G) \vert \geq p$.
Step 2. By Lagrange's theorem, $\vert Z(G) \vert$ is $p$ or $p^2$. If it is $p^2$, then $Z(G) = G$ and $G$ is abelian. If $\vert Z(G) \vert = p$, then $G / Z(G)$ has order $p$, so it is cyclic (problem of 9 September 2026). By the problem of 14 October 2026, $G$ is then abelian, so $Z(G) = G$, contradicting $\vert Z(G) \vert = p \lt p^2$. So this case cannot occur.
Hence $G$ is abelian. (In fact $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$ or $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_p \times \mathbb{Z}_p$.)

problems.title: If a group has exactly one element of order $2$, that element is central
problems.problem:
Let $G$ be a group with exactly one element $a$ of order $2$.
  1. Prove that $a \in Z(G)$, that is, $ag = ga$ for every $g \in G$.
  2. Give an example of a nonabelian group with exactly one element of order $2$.
  3. Show that a finite abelian group $G$ of even order with exactly one element $a$ of order $2$ satisfies $\prod_{g \in G} g = a$.
problems.hint:
• Conjugation preserves order: $(gag^{-1})^k = g a^k g^{-1}$.
  • For (b), look at the quaternion group $Q_8$. For (c), pair each element with its inverse.
problems.solution:
(a) Let $g \in G$ and $b = g a g^{-1}$. Then $b^2 = g a^2 g^{-1} = e$, and $b \neq e$ (otherwise $a = g^{-1} e g = e$). So $b$ has order $2$, and by uniqueness $b = a$. Thus $g a g^{-1} = a$, i.e. $ga = ag$, for every $g$, and $a \in Z(G)$.
(b) The quaternion group $Q_8 = \{ \pm 1, \pm i, \pm j, \pm k \}$ with $i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1$ is nonabelian ($ij = k$ but $ji = -k$). Its elements $\pm i, \pm j, \pm k$ have order $4$, $1$ has order $1$, and $-1$ is the only element of order $2$. As (a) predicts, $Z(Q_8) = \{ \pm 1 \}$ contains it.
(c) In the product $\prod_{g \in G} g$ (well defined since $G$ is abelian), group each $g$ with $g \neq g^{-1}$ together with $g^{-1}$; each such pair contributes $g g^{-1} = e$. The elements left over satisfy $g = g^{-1}$, i.e. $g^2 = e$; these are $e$ and the elements of order $2$, which here are just $e$ and $a$. So the product is $e \cdot a = a$.
Example: Wilson's theorem. For a prime $p$, the group $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is abelian of order $p - 1$, and $x^2 = 1$ forces $p \mid (x - 1)(x + 1)$, so $-1$ is its only element of order $2$ (for $p > 2$). Part (c) gives $(p - 1)! \equiv -1 \pmod p$.
